en-Yoruba-yo-name-t42iynxd.etymologyText:
Of unclear and disputed origin, it is likely that it was derived from an exonym from neighboring groups to the north, such as Hausa, Fulani, or Bariba. Various implausible etymologies have been proposed, often used to insult the Yoruba people or support supposed Middle Eastern or Jewish origins of the Yoruba people. What is certain is that the term was used originally in reference to only the Ọ̀yọ́ people (a subgroup of the Yoruba ethnic group) and the Oyo empire, and did not become used to refer to all Yoruba peoples until the late 19th century during attempts to foster a common ethnic identity. Etymological theories include:
* Several folk etymologies associate the term from coming from Hausa or Fula slurs of Yoruba people, such as Hausa ya rība meaning "One who cheats," referring to the supposed deceitful tactics Yoruba traders used, or Hausa ya ruba meaning "Bad or rotten person." These have been dismissed and proscribed by most Yoruba scholars, however, the Yoruba term yóóbá is derived from the first etymology, but is not to be mistaken with "Yoruba."
*According to linguist Kọlá Túbọ̀sún, it ultimately derives from a contraction of yārṑ + ọba "Children of the Ọba", (referring to the Alaafin of Oyo).
* A newly proposed theory suggests it is a reborrowing from the word Yàgbà, a Yoruba subethnic group, borrowed into the Nupe and Hausa languages, where it became Yarba, and then reborrowed from Hausa Yarbanci

Those in the current Nigerian state of Ekiti may use kàbí or ubi sí, in addition to kàríbi. In the Akure subdialect of Ekiti, they mainly use kàríbi, in addition to kàí or kàbí. All these terms are synonymous and can generally used by any Ekiti speaker regardless of subdialect. The term kàrí is also used in Ijesha.

en-ede-yo-noun-pO8wS6Qq.etymologyText: Ultimately from Proto-Yoruba *è-dè. While the semantic meaning of language and this specific form is restricted to Proto-Yoruba, the root is widespread across Niger-Congo as roots for "tongue," and thus derives from an older stem. That older stem may be Proto-Yoruboid *-dè. The stem likely originally meant tongue, language, and the general mouth area, but became restricted for language (and also became the term for lip), and replaced ohùn. This is almost certainly a Doublet of ètè. This also explains why the Proto-Yoruboid word for tongue is likely an innovation, see *ʊ́-ɓã́ (“tongue”), see ahọ́n (“tongue”). Compare with Proto-Edoid *U-dhamhɪ, Ibibio edeme, Proto-Bantu *dʊ̀dɪ́mì, Proto-Jukunoid *dema. Many other Yoruba-dialects also have different terms for the language, see eréùn in Ijebu.

en-kiniun-yo-noun-~FlIdxK7.etymologyText:
Compare with Ifè kìnìwú. It is not related to almost any Volta-Niger roots for lion, and cognates do not exist in other Proto-Edekiri or Proto-Yoruba descended languages spoken east of the Yoruba homeland, such as Itsekiri, Olukumi, or Igala. Its relation to Fon kinikíní, Gun kinnikinni, Aja (East Africa) kinnikinni, as well as the significance of the "lion" in the cultures of Gbe-speaking peoples, but a lack of significance of the lion in Yorubaland (compared to the leopard) because of its absence in the tropical forests of most of Yorubaland (words for "lion" do not exist in many Niger-delta languages, as well as in Ayere or Ukaan), may explain why a native root did not persist. Thus, perhaps this comes from any of the various Gbe-roots, which was then borrowed and spread east across the forest among Yoruba-dialects, and then ending at the savanna (where native or locally derived terms for lion would exist).
See Proto-Yoruba *kɪ̃̀nɪ̃̀wṹ, while this term is shared between many Yoruba dialects, but a single form cannot be formally reconstructed to the level of Proto-Yoruboid because of linguistic considerations.

A possible wider distribution may exist, see Benue-Congo languages Ibibio ebot, Proto-Plateau *-buon (2a), Proto-Plateau *ì-bu (2b), and Proto-Plateau *-bwal (3), and maybe even Baatonum boo.

en-oriṣa-yo-noun-JduUEHxK.etymologyText:
From Òrìṣà. The precise etymology of the term is unknown, (possibly from Proto-Yoruboid *Ò-rìsà, Proto-Yoruboid *ɔ̀-rɪ̀cà, or Proto-Yoruboid *Ò-rìcà), but several folk etymologies exist, the main one suggesting it comes from orí (“head, conscience, destiny”) + ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + ṣà (“to be selected, to choose”), literally “The head that is specially selected”. (This is unlikely though as this term only fits the Yoruba definition of òrìṣà, but not the cognate versions in other languages or even in other Yoruba dialects).
The term òrìṣà, which is a general name for all deities in the Yoruba religion, likely derived from the proper noun form Òrìṣà, in reference to a specific arch-divinity of the sky and creation (now known as Òrìṣàńlá and Ọbàtálá). In other related languages, and some dialects of the Yoruba language, the cognate term has retained its proper noun definition, referring to a specific high-ranking male divinity associated with the sky, creation, and government. These cognates include Itsekiri Òrìtsẹ̀, Igbo Òlìsà, Urhobo Oyise, Èkìtì Yoruba Ọ̀rị̀ṣà, Ọ̀wọ̀ Yoruba Òrìchà, Edo Osa, Oisa, Ebira Oricha, and Fon Lisà

en-Ogun-yo-name-EL846R5-.etymologyText:
From *ògún (“spirit or energy one has after hunting or battling”), ultimately from Proto-Yoruboid *ò-gwṹ, equivalent ò- + gún.
* The concept of Ogun as the embodiment of iron and hunting likely dates to the Iron Age and is thus present in most religious/spiritual practices of Volta-Niger and Benue-Congo speaking peoples. Two groups of cognates exist. The first ones are those in which this spirit is personified as a deity and becoming a proper noun, see Edo Ogun and Fon Gu. However, other cognates maintain the noun form of this word as simply the energy or spirit associated with killing, see Igala ògwú (“killer instinct”), Idoma ògwú (“honor given to a successful hunter or warrior; display of behavior when someone has killed a large animal”), or possibly Igbo òdogwu (“mighty hunter”). The root term *gwṹ could be cognate with Volta-Niger language terms for "kill," see Igbo ògbú (“killer”) or perhaps nwụ (“to kill”), Proto-Edoid *ghu, Nupe wu, Ibibio woot, Akan wu, Kamo yu. This is likely especially since Igala égwú means "corpse," and the term also greatly resembles the verb to die in Yorùbá, kú.
Likely a Doublet of Egúngún, referring to deified ancestors and veneration of the dead, see Proto-Yoruboid *É-gwṹ.

glosses: Ogun (orisha of war, iron, metallurgy, and technology), patron of warriors, hunters, blacksmiths, and ironworkers.

en-oni--yo-prefix-nTGMUeCG.etymologyText: From o- (“nominalizing prefix”) + ní (“to have; to own”). The "o" prefix harmonizes with the initial vowel associated with the noun it precedes. en-ọkan-yo-noun-OowwC5zp.etymologyText: Likely a Proto-Yoruba innovation that displaced ẹ̀dọ̀ (“chest, heart, emotion”), which served as the term for the organ for the seat of emotion (heart). In Northwest Yoruba and Standard Yoruba, this term semantically shifted to "liver," while certain Yoruba dialects maintain the semantic meaning of ẹ̀dọ̀ "emotion, feeling." However, almost all Yoruba dialects refer to the heart organ as "ọkàn," suggesting that it was a Proto-Yoruba innovation, see Proto-Yoruba *ɔ-kã̀, with it likely not existing in Proto-Edekiri. Yoruba dialects like Southeast Yoruba not descended from Proto-Yoruba likely thus borrowed the word from nearby Proto-Yoruba speakers. Evidence of pre-Yoruba roots may be found in a possible cognate, Olukumi akan (“kidney”), suggesting the term may have been a general root for internal organs, in a similar fashion to the word fùkù.

en-Egungun-yo-noun-rKrAO-D1.etymologyText:
Folk etymology from the Odù Ifá (corpus of the Yoruba religion), specifically Ọ̀wọ́nrinṣẹ́ (Odu #105), states it comes from e- (“agent creating prefix”) + gún (“to arrive, to land”) + gún (“to align, to straighten, to put in order”), literally “the ones who arrive to put (the world) in order”. Said to be associated with the phrase sayégún (“One who aligns the world”).
Cognate with Ede Nago egoúngoún, Igala égwú, Igala Égwú. In Igala, the term in its noun form means corpse or dead body. This suggests that it comes from the same root as Igala ògwú (“killer instinct, spirit associated with killing”), in which the root gwú, likely means to kill or die. Thus, this term is proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *é-gwṹ, ultimately deriving from Proto-Yoruboid *gwú (“to die”). This is the same root that the term Ògún is believed to come from, thus making this a Doublet of Ògún. The root gwú in term is almost certainly from the same root as kú (“to die”), see *kú for its relation to other languages.

en-Olodumare-yo-name-oPqF4e70.etymologyText:
From oní- + òdùmarè. Many folk etymologies attempt to explain the origin of the term òdùmàrè, but the etymology is ultimately unclear
*A chapter from the Odù Ifa (Yoruba religious text), Ọ̀sá Ògúndá, explains that the etymology comes from the phrase oní odù tí ń tan òṣùmàrè, ultimately from oní- (“one who has”) + odù (“pot”) + òṣùmàrè (“rainbow”), literally “The owner of the pot from which the rainbow comes from”
*Another folk etymology explains it as ultimately meaning odù (“source of creation, pot”) + mà (“does not”) + rè (“to become exhausted, empty”), literally “The Owner of the Source of Creation that does not get exhausted; The All Sufficient One”
* Compare with Òṣùmàrè
*Another theory tends to link the term to àrè, referring to a stranger or someone of unknown background, referring to the mysterious origins associated with Olodumare, thus breaking down to oní- (“one who has”) + òdù (“pot, source”) + mọ̀ (“to know”) + àrè (“stranger, foreigner, of unknown background”)

glosses: A primordial being of creation in the Yoruba pantheon, regarded as the supreme ruler of the universe and the highest ranking divinity of Ìṣẹ̀ṣe

It is unclear but possible that this is also attested in NWY, or it is possible it is related to imí. The term "imi," has a much wider etymology with cognates found throughout Volta-Niger, so it is unlikely that only NWY maintained the word. glosses: Oko (orisha), the orisha of farming and agriculture, in his male form, he is regarded as a sorcerer. The root, oṣó (“sorcerer”) in many names among the Ẹ̀gbá and Ìjẹ̀bú refers to Oko.
nonstandard spelling of Gáḿbíà (“Gambia (a country in West Africa)”)
nonstandard spelling of Gáḿbíà (“River Gambia (a river in West Africa)”)

en-alubọsa-yo-noun-KIlxZxaF.etymologyText: From Hausa albasa, ultimately from Arabic بَصَل (baṣal). Cognates with Emai àlùbásà

en-adiẹ-yo-noun-gR64G50R.etymologyText: Cognate with Ìjẹ̀bú Yoruba ẹdùwẹ, proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *á-dɪ̀wɛ, compare with Yoruba ẹyẹ.

glosses: good health, peace (often used in salutations)

examples.translation: How are you?

en-alubarika-yo-noun-WI08~zEW.etymologyText: From Hausa àlbar̃kā̀, ultimately from Arabic بَرَكَة (baraka). Doublet of báríkà.

examples.text: Olúwa yóò fi àlùbàríkà sí iṣẹ́ẹ wa
examples.translation: May the Lord add a blessing to our work

en-alujọnnu-yo-noun-HjQ6Nyl4.etymologyText: From Hausa àljan, from Arabic جَانّ (jānn).

glosses: jinn, imp, malevolent spirit, a person with special powers

en-alangba-yo-noun-uVy8~gzS.etymologyText: Possibly from oní- (“one who has”) + à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + ǹ + gbá (“to sway, to strut while walking”), literally “The one who sways while walking”

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: to sway, to strut while walking

en-aṣiri-yo-noun-K7gNU3sd.etymologyText: From Hausa àsīr̃ī, ultimately from Arabic سِرّ (sirr).

en-ayọ-yo-noun-sRNAW2-R.etymologyText: a- (“agent prefix”) + yọ̀ (“to rejoice”). Cognates include Itsekiri ọ̀yọ̀, Ede Idaca ayɔ̀

examples.text: Orin ayọ̀ ló ń dùn lẹ́ẹ̀kan yẹn
examples.translation: Joyful music was playing a short while ago

en-ehoro-yo-noun-Lb0L6wOW.etymologyText: Perhaps related to Igala áfolo, compare with Ifè aworo, proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *á-folo

glosses: rabbit, hare; (in particular) African savanna hare

en-erinmi-yo-noun-2zX7RdHr.etymologyText: From erin (“elephant”) + omi (“water”), literally “water elephant”, see Urhobo eníame

en-eṣinṣin-yo-noun-boOaycX2.etymologyText: Proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *V́-cĩcĩ, cognate with Igala áchichi, Olukumi esinsin, Ifè etsĩtsĩ, see Yoruboid reconstruction for more, likely also related to English tsetse, Tswana tsêtsê.

en-maluu-yo-noun-AOE4MQIf.etymologyText: Possibly from an older form màlúwù. It is a very old loan word, likely from a language of what is now Northern Nigeria (as that is how cows likely arrived to Yorubaland, perhaps from Fula. Cognate words do not exist or have not been found in the modern vocabulary of Northern languages that have vocabulary borrowed by the Yoruba (Baatonum, Fulfulde, Hausa, Nupe), thus possibly suggesting it may have likely borrowed from a now extinct language, or a word no longer used in the vocabulary of the original language.

glosses: cow, ox, cattle; (in particular) zebu cow

en-oju_odu-yo-noun-3t~GXk5l.etymologyText: From ojú (“eye, main, center”) + odù (“Odu Ifa”), literally “The main Odu”.

glosses: one of the sixteen principal signs of the Ifa divination system
The first and most important sixteen chapters of the odù Ifá
one of the two hundred and forty minor signs of the Ifa divination system

en-Ifa-yo-noun-9uhfavsw.etymologyText: From Proto-Yoruboid *ɪ́-fá, Ifa divination can be traced linguistically to Volta-Niger, see Proto-Volta-Niger *-fa, however the ultimately etymology of the root is of unknown origin. Cognates exist across Volta-Niger languages, see Igbo Afa, Ewe Afá, Fon Fá, Igala Ífá, Edo Iha, Ebira Eva, Urhobo Epha, and Nupe Eba. Several theories exist among worshippers of Ifá

glosses: A complex system of divination in Yoruba religion.

en-Ifa-yo-name-SDleLQX-.etymologyText: From Proto-Yoruboid *ɪ́-fá, Ifa divination can be traced linguistically to Volta-Niger, see Proto-Volta-Niger *-fa, however the ultimately etymology of the root is of unknown origin. Cognates exist across Volta-Niger languages, see Igbo Afa, Ewe Afá, Fon Fá, Igala Ífá, Edo Iha, Ebira Eva, Urhobo Epha, and Nupe Eba. Several theories exist among worshippers of Ifá

glosses: the spirit associated with divination, wisdom, and the oracle

en-Ọọni-yo-name-PBm9NZPf.etymologyText: Etymology is unknown, the deletion of the /w/ (also /ɣ/) phoneme in the Ifẹ̀ and Èkìtì dialects of Yoruba may suggest the original form as Proto-Yoruba Proto-Yoruba *ɔ̀-ɣɔ̀nɪ̃, equivalent to ọ̀ọ̀ (“respect”) + ọni (“person”). Cognate with Edo Ọ́ghẹ̀nnẹ́ and Urhobo Ọ́ghẹ̀nẹ́, where the term is also used in reference to a Supreme being synonymous with Odùduwà

glosses: the title of the traditional monarch of the town of Ifẹ (Ifẹ̀) and the Ifẹ̀ people, they are regarded as one the highest ranking Yoruba monarchs, and is the chief priest of the worship of Odùduwà
Oduduwa as a divine supernatural deity

derivedTerms.english: god king, a praise name for the Ọ̀ọ̀ni

en-Ọya-yo-name-tl6AnpEb.etymologyText: A common folk etymology links her name to ọ- (“agent prefix”) + ya (“to tear, to rip open”), literally “She tore”, referring to her representation as violent whirlwinds. Also possibly from aya (“wife”), as she is strongly associated as the wife of Ṣàngó

glosses: A female orisha and one of the irúnmọlẹ̀ in the Yoruba religion, she is believed to be the spirit of the Niger river, and is the goddess of storms, winds. She is the wife of Ṣàngó, and was also an ayaba (“queen”), when he was the Aláàfin of Ọ̀yọ́.

examples.text: She is regarded as the favorite of Ṣàngó's wife because of their similar tempers.
Ọyá pé méjì. Ọya kìíní ni èyí tí ó bá àwọn Irúnmọlẹ̀ wá sí ayé; èkejì sì ni Ọya tí ó jẹ́ ìyàwóo Ṣàngó Ìtí-olú Olúkòso tíí ṣe Aláàfin ní Ọyọ́-ilé
examples.translation: There are two forms of Oya. The first Oya is the primordial deity who accompanied the four hundred other deities to earth, and the second is Oya the orisha who was the wife of Shango the Alaafin of Oyo

glosses: Niger (a major river in West Africa that flows into the Gulf of Guinea in Nigeria)

derivedTerms.english: A devotee or priest of Ọya
Chanting and invocations during the praise of Ọya
A Yoruba name meaning Ọya has given birth to this child
A Yoruba name meaning Ọya blessed me
A Yoruba name meaning Ọya received honor
A Yoruba name meaning Ọya has favored me
A Yoruba name meaning Ọya is worthy of praise
The northern region of Nigeria, the region of Nigeria above the Niger river

glosses: The seventeenth sign of the Ifa divination system, it is the first and most important, of the signs of the ọmọ odù; the 240 minor signs
The seventeenth chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus. It is one of the sixteen chapters in the Ogbè category (àpólà) and the first and most important of the 240 minor chapters, or àmúlù of the Odù Ifá.
The spirit associated with this chapter

en-Ogbe-yo-name-If2QLR04.etymologyText: Cognate terms are found throughout Volta-Niger languages, and cognates also show evidence of the o- and e- prefixes, which are likely obsolete plural markers. See Itsekiri Ogbìn, Igala Ébì, Edo Ógbì, Igbo Ógbì, Igbo Óbì (Nsukka), Idoma Ébì, Fon Gbè, proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *ó-gbì. In sister divination systems, this signature is known as Osika, Osinkan, and Osinkara.

glosses: The first principal sign of the Ifa divination system.
The first of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the Odù Ifá, consisting of the first principal chapter, (Èjì Ogbè) and the other fifteen chapters of Ogbè.
The first and most important chapter of the Odù Ifá
The spirit and divinity associated with the Ogbè divination sign, he is believed to be a son of Ọ̀ṣun and Ọ̀rúnmìlà and was born in the town of Ọ̀tùn, where the king was his maternal grandfather.

en-Ọyẹku-yo-name-NLQYz26A.etymologyText: Folk etymology suggests it comes from ọ̀- (“nominalizing prefix”) + yẹ̀ (“to avoid, to dodge”) + ikú (“death”), literally “That which avoids death”. It is a possibility that the root term may relate to kú (to die) as the second part of the term stays relatively consistently throughout Volta-Niger languages, and kwu or ku is generally associated with old roots for death, however, in some cognate terms, it changes, so that assertion is unlikely, but possible. See Gun Ìyẹ̀kú, Itsekiri Akú, Igala Ọyẹkwu, Igala Akwu, Edo Àkó, Urhobo Àkó, Igbo Àhwụ, Nupe Eyako, Ebira Ọ̀hàkú. Proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *V-kwú

glosses: The second principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The second of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the Odù Ifá, consisting of the second principal chapter, (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (beginning with Ọ̀yẹ̀kúlógbè).
The second chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù
The spirit and divinity associated with the Ọ̀yẹ̀kú divination sign

en-Iwori-yo-name-RisU2EF0.etymologyText: From Proto-Yoruboid *ò-ɣòlì, across Volta-Niger, the term has not changed from what could be its original form where, making it potentially possible to reconstruct the root all the way to Proto-Volta-Niger, (see Proto-Volta-Niger *-ɣòlì or Proto-Volta-Niger *-gòlì). Cognate with Igala Ògòlì, Itsekiri Òɣòlì, Edo Òɣòì, Urhobo Òɣòrì, Igbo Ògori (Nsuka), Igbo Òyori (Nri), Nupe Gòrì, Gun Wolì.

glosses: The third principal sign of the Ifa divination system

examples.text: èèwọ̀ ni, Ìwòrì kì í rẹ̀kú, eégun kò gbọ́dọ̀ na babaláwo
examples.translation: It is a taboo, Iwori does not carry an egúngún costume; an egúngún must not beat an Ifá priest

glosses: The third of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the Odù Ifá, consisting of the third principal chapter, (Ìwòrì Méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Ìwòrì.
The third chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù
The spirit and divinity associated with the Ìwòrì divination sign

en-Odi-yo-name-GZGwYUwW.etymologyText:
Cognate across Volta-Niger, where it has consistently remained constant across almost all the languages, making it potentially possible to reconstruct the root all the way to Proto-Volta-Niger, (see Proto-Volta-Niger *-dí). Cognate with Igala Òjí, ultimately derived from Proto-Yoruboid *Ò-dí, see there for more cognates.
* Folk etymologies found in the verses assigned to this chapter are plentiful for example, ò- (“nominalizing prefix”) + dí (“to block”), literally “That which blocks evil”.

glosses: The fourth principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The fourth of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the odù Ifá, consisting of the fourth principal chapter, (Òdí méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Òdí.
The fourth chapter of the odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù
The spirit associated with the Òdí sign, he is believed to have born in a place near Ìlọrin

en-Irosun-yo-name-VecTt73O.etymologyText: Possibly, but unlikely from ìròsùn (“camwood”). Cognate with Idoma Orosu, Itsekiri Ùròsùn, Igala Òlòrù, Edo Òrúùhù, Urhobo Ùɹ̝̊ùɹ̝̊ù, Igbo Ùrúrù, Igbo Ùlúshù, Nupe Rùsù, Ebira Òròsù, Fon Lósò. Proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *ò-lòsũ̀, it has remained consistent across Volta-Niger, with the exception of the variation between /s/, /r/, and /h/, a common occurrence. Perhaps ultimately from a root similar to Proto-Volta-Niger *-lòsù

glosses: The fifth principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The fifth of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the odù Ifá, consisting of the fifth principal chapter, (Ìrosùn méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Ìrosùn.
The fifth chapter of the odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù
The spirit associated with the Ìrosùn sign, he is believed to have born in the town of Ìdèrè in the Ìbàràpá Yoruba region
The sixth principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The sixth of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the Odù Ifá, consisting of the sixth principal chapter, (Ọ̀wọ́nrín méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Ọ̀wọ́nrín
The sixth chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù
The spirit associated with the Ọ̀wọ́nrín sign, believed to have been born in the Kétu region.

en-Ọbara-yo-name-w0IUTgoi.etymologyText: Cognate across Volta-Niger, the term has remained relatively constant across all the languages in that group, making it potentially possible to reconstruct the root all the way to Proto-Volta-Niger, (see Proto-Volta-Niger *-bàlà). Cognate with Igala Ọ̀bàlà, Itsekiri Ọ̀bàrà, ultimately derived from Proto-Yoruboid *ɔ̀-bàlà, see there for more cognates.

glosses: The seventh principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The seventh of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the odù Ifá, consisting of the seventh principal chapter, (Ọ̀bàrà méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Ọ̀bàrà
The seventh chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù
The spirit associated with the Ọ̀bàrà sign

en-Ọkanran-yo-name-6vEYqs-s.etymologyText: Possibly from ọ̀kàn (“heart, mind, soul”) + ràn (“to help, to aid”), literally “The soul helps”, from a folk etymology. Cognate with Idoma Okana

glosses: The eighth principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The eighth of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the odù Ifá, consisting of the eighth principal chapter, (Ọ̀kànràn méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Ọ̀kànràn
The eighth chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù

en-Ogunda-yo-name-ptR9tcEy.etymologyText: An ancient term associated with the majority of the Ifa-divination systems of other Volta-Niger groups. Proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *ò-gʷṹtã́, where it has a synonymous name Èjítọ́n, used currently in Yoruba only in the Ekiti dialect, but is regarded as this term in other languages. See Igala Ògwútọ, Igbo Ògúte, Nupe Gúta, Ebira Ògútá, Gun Ègúdá, Fon Gùdá, ultimately from a common Volta-Niger root, perhaps Proto-Volta-Niger *-gúta, but the etymology is not known beyond there. Folk etymologies associate with the deity Yoruba Ògún, which could suggest a link to Igala ògwú.

glosses: The ninth principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The ninth of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the odù Ifá, consisting of the ninth principal chapter, (Ògúndá méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Ògúndá
The ninth chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù

en-Ọsa-yo-name-grlhORFj.etymologyText: Compare with Igala Ọ̀rá, Itsekiri Ọ̀sá, proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *Ɔ̀-sá, see there for cognates across Volta-Niger

glosses: The tenth principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The tenth of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the odù Ifá, consisting of the tenth principal chapter, (Ọ̀sá méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Ọ̀sá
The tenth chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù

en-Ika-yo-name-t5yxKJ-2.etymologyText: Cognate across Volta-Niger, where it the term has remained relatively constant across all the languages, making it potentially possible to reconstruct the root all the way to Proto-Volta-Niger, (see Proto-Volta-Niger *-ká). Cognate with Igala Ẹ̀ká, Itsekiri Ẹ̀ká ultimately derived from Proto-Yoruboid *ɛ̀-ká, see there for more cognates.

glosses: The eleventh principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The eleventh of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the odù Ifá, consisting of the eleventh principal chapter, (Ìká méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Ìká
The eleventh chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù

en-Otuurupọn-yo-name-acuIggcn.etymologyText: Cognate terms across Volta-Niger, the term has not changed from what could be its original form where, making it potentially possible to reconstruct the root all the way to Proto-Volta-Niger, (see Proto-Volta-Niger *-túrúkpà). Cognate with Igala Àtúnúkpà, Itsekiri Àtúkpà, ultimately derived from Proto-Yoruboid *À-túlúkpɔ̃̀, see there for more cognates.

glosses: The twelfth principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The twelfth of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the Odù Ifá, consisting of the twelfth principal chapter, (Òtúúrúpọ̀n méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Òtúúrúpọ̀n.
The twelfth chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù
alternative form of Òtúrá (“The thirteenth principal sign of the Ifa divination system and thirteenth chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus”)
The fourteenth principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The fourteenth of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the Odù Ifá, consisting of the fourteenth principal chapter, (Ìrẹ̀tẹ̀ méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Ìrẹ̀tẹ̀.
The fourteenth chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù
The spirit and divinity associated with the Ìrẹtẹ̀ divination sign.

en-Ọsẹ-yo-name-nzn-a69d.etymologyText: Possibly from ọ̀- (“nominalizing prefix”) + sẹ́ (“to snap, to break, to deny”), cognate with Idoma Oche

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: to snap, to break, to deny

glosses: The fifteenth principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The fifteenth of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the Odù Ifá, consisting of the fifteenth principal chapter, (Ọ̀sẹ́ méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Ọ̀sẹ́.
The fifteenth chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus, and one of the major ojú odù
The spirit and divinity associated with the Ọ̀sẹ́ divination sign

en-Ofun-yo-name-ySket1d8.etymologyText: Cognate across Volta-Niger, the term has remained relatively constant across all the languages in that group, making it potentially possible to reconstruct the root all the way to Proto-Volta-Niger, (see Proto-Volta-Niger *-fú). Cognate with Igala Òfú, Itsekiri Òfún, ultimately derived from Proto-Yoruboid *Ò-fṹ, see there for more cognates.

glosses: The sixteenth principal sign of the Ifa divination system
The sixteenth and final of the àpólà or sixteen categories in the Odù Ifá, consisting of the final principal chapter, (Òfún méjì) and the other fifteen chapters of Òfún.
The sixteenth chapter of the Odù Ifá corpus, and the last of the major ojú odù
The spirit and divinity associated with the Òfún divination sign
A Yoruba subethnic group whom live in the city of Savè.
A Yoruba dialect spoken by the Ṣábẹ̀ẹ́ people

derivedTerms.english: the king of the Ṣábẹ̀ẹ́ people

en-Ajaṣẹ-yo-name-OVsSE7Rb.etymologyText: From à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + jà (“to fight”) + ṣẹ́ (“to be victorious”).

glosses: a name for several towns in Yorubaland. The towns are often suffixed by a unique identifying term as a way of differentiating them.
Àjàṣẹ́ people, a subgroup of the Yoruba people who live in the town of Porto-Novo and who speak the Àjàṣẹ́ dialect of Yoruba
a name for several towns in Yorubaland. The towns are often suffixed by a unique identifying term as a way of differentiating them.
The dialect of the Yoruba language spoken in the town of Àjàṣẹ́ (Porto-Novo).
a name for several towns in Yorubaland. The towns are often suffixed by a unique identifying term as a way of differentiating them.

en-Eko-yo-name-~SdG3jcg.etymologyText: From Edo Eko (“Lagos”), from Edo eko (“temporary camp”).

glosses: A Yoruba dialect spoken in Lagos by the people of Èkó

en-Abẹokuta-yo-name-uiAYIXRY.etymologyText: From abẹ́ (“under”) + òkúta (“rock (referring to the Olúmọ rock)”), literally “Under the rock”.

en-Ọṣun-yo-name-HJMj--3Y.etymologyText: From ọ̀- (“nominalizing prefix”) + ṣun (“to ooze, to flow from”), literally “The one who water flows from”.

glosses: Oshun, an orisha in Yoruba religion, she is regarded as the Yoruba deity of fertility, freshwater, love, beauty, motherhood, healing, and jewelry, and is the spirit of the Osun river.

examples.text: Ìṣẹ́lẹ̀rú àgbo, àgbàrá àgbo, l'Ọ̀ṣún fi ń womọ ọ rẹ̀ kí dókítà ó tóó dé
examples.translation: The freshwater turned into a potion, the drainage water turned into a potion, this is was what Ọ̀ṣun used to cure her children before western doctors arrived

en-Ọyọ-yo-name-~PTeFFBy.etymologyText: Folk etymology states it comes from ọ̀- (nominalizing prefix) + yọ́ (“to slide off”), literally “The place that we slide off of (in reference to the slipperiness of the ground)”.

glosses: A Yoruba subethnic group who speaks the Ọ̀yọ́ dialect

examples.text: The Ọ̀yọ́ they were the first Yoruba speaking group to be referred to by the name "Yoruba"

glosses: a dialect of the Yoruba language spoken by the Ọ̀yọ́ people, it serves as the basis for the modern Standard Yoruba koine (Yorùbá Àjùmọ̀lò)
Oyo (a city in Nigeria), the modern city of Ọ̀yọ́ founded after the destruction of Ọ̀yọ́-Ilé
Old Oyo, the capital of the Ọ̀yọ́ empire until its destruction during the Eleduwe War, (Ogun Elédùwẹ̀) in 1835

derivedTerms.english: The ancient capital of the Ọ̀yọ́ empire
A senior class of chiefs of the Ọ̀yọ́ empire that served as advisors to the Aláàfin

en-Ijẹbu-Ode-yo-name-LRpGi8qU.etymologyText: From Ìjẹ̀bú (“Ijebu”) + òde (“town”), literally “The town of the Ìjẹ̀bú”

en-Ifẹ-yo-name-DVhPPzys.etymologyText:
From Ufẹ̀. Several folk etymologies existed including i- (“nominalizing prefix”) + fẹ̀ + [Term?] (“to widen, to spread”), literally “The Land that widens”
*Possibly from i- (“nominalizing prefix”) + fẹ̀ (“to be prosperous, to be successful”), literally “Land of prosperity”

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: to be prosperous, to be successful

glosses: mythological origin place of the Yoruba people
Ife, a subgroup of the Yoruba people, who speak the Ifẹ̀ dialect of Yoruba
A dialect of the Yoruba language

en-Ogbomọṣọ-yo-name-JjN859yi.etymologyText: Several folk etymologies exist, one of which suggests ògbó (“a type of sword”) + mọ̀ (“to know, to be familiar with”) + ọ̀- (“nominalizing prefix”) + ṣọ́ (“to protect”), literally “The ogbo sword knows how to protect”

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: to know, to be familiar with

en-Ilọrin-yo-name-iqiLmAJm.etymologyText: A common folk etymology suggests, ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + lọ̀ (“to grind”) + irin (“iron”), literally “The place where iron is processed”

glosses: A Yoruba dialect spoken by the Ìlọrin people

en-Oṣogbo-yo-name-dFbmMVpL.etymologyText: Folk etymology states it comes from oṣó (“sorcerer”) + igbó (“forest”), literally “Sorcerer of the forest”, however this is unlikely the real etymology

en-Ileṣa-yo-name-TIM5wfCb.etymologyText: Original term in the Ijesha dialect is Uléṣà. en-Ejigbo-yo-name-nXkBQSva.etymologyText: There is some historical significance to the name of this town, it features in a legendary ancient market of Ifẹ̀, Èjìgbòmẹkùn, which features prominently in Yoruba oral history. In addition, several other locations throughout Yorubaland bear an alternate version of the name, Ìjìgbò, which is almost always used interchangeably with Èjìgbò. Èjìgbòmẹkùn in Ifẹ̀ oral tradition is regarded as the first market in Ifẹ̀, is closely associated with many Yoruba divinities, including Ajé, Ọ̀rúnmìlà, and features prominently in many verses of the Odù Ifá. While there is a clear relationship between the name Èjìgbòmẹkùn and the locations known as Èjìgbò or Ìjìgbò, the historical relationship between them are not clear, except that like many Yorùbá towns, most ones named Èjìgbò claim to be descended from Ifẹ̀. The name Ùgbòmẹkùn, an ancient name for the region that is now Ifẹ̀, is also clearly related. Thus, a link between Èjìgbò and the Ùgbò people has also been hypothesized, which is the most common explanation for ancient Ifẹ̀ terms with "gbò," see Ọ̀ṣẹ̀rẹ̀màgbò.

This semantic meaning seems to still exist in compound terms like ọlọ́jà (“king”), literally meaning "ruler of the town." The meaning of the verb *jɔ́ could relate to the traditional significance of the symbolic of the sunrise and the "beginning," that the day brings. en-agbọn-yo-noun-I-vOcsRC.etymologyText:
Unclear etymology, from à- + gbọn, likely a Yoruba coinage as the words for coconut in Central Yoruba or related languages like Itsekiri, Igala, Edo, Igbo, Nupe, are not related from this (most come from a Portuguese root). Other languages that don't have borrowings from Portuguese usually use a variation or compounding with a word for the oil palm tree, which is similar to the coconut. This may also suggest that Western Yoruba speakers did not receive coconuts from the Portuguese, and instead may have gotten it from another source. Compare with Ifè àgbã.
*Unlikely, but possibly from à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + gbọ̀n (“to shake”)?

en-agbọn-yo-noun-S-63LeWL.etymologyText: Proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *à-gbã̀. Cognates exist in most other Volta-Niger languages (where it is often translated as chin or jaw), suggesting what is likely a common Volta-Niger origin, see Igala àgbà, Ayere àngbà, Yekhee agba, Itsekiri agba, Arigidi àmgbà, Arigidi àgbɔ̀̃, Edo agbanmwẹn, Idoma agba, Fon gbà, Igbo àgbà, and Urhobo egba, and potentially Oko-Eni-Osayen akã̂, perhaps from Proto-Volta-Niger *à-gbà. The possible Benue-Congo cognates Ibibio mban̄, Ahwai akpaal, and Ahwai áŋkpàn may suggest a pre-Volta-Niger origin, which is uncertain.

examples.translation: Which page did we read last? — We read the twentieth page last.

derivedTerms.english: one hundred and ninety; two hundred

en-ogun-yo-noun-vTB2M22N.etymologyText: Cognates include Ifè ogú and Igala ógwú, from Proto-Yoruboid *ó-gwṹ.

examples.translation: inheritance tax
Anyone who builds his hope on some future legacy will become vulnerable to destitution. (proverb against irrational expectation)

examples.text: Mo ń kọ́ lìǹgúísíìkì ní yunifásitì ti Ìbàdàn.
examples.translation: I'm studying linguistics at the University of Ibadan.

glosses: abbreviation of àti bẹ́ẹ̀ bẹ́ẹ̀ lọ (“et cetera; and so on”)
Used after a noun to signify "What about...?"

examples.text: Mo wà dáadáa o! Ẹ̀yin ńkọ́?
examples.translation: I'm doing well! And you?

glosses: Used after a noun to signify "Where is...?"

examples.text: Mo wà dáadáa o! Ẹ̀yin ńkọ́?
examples.translation: I'm doing well! And you?

glosses: Used after a noun to signify "What about...?"

examples.translation: What about you?

glosses: Used after a noun to signify "Where is...?"

examples.translation: Where is your wife?

en-igba-yo-noun-XZnCLZAH.etymologyText: From Proto-Yoruboid *ʊ́-gbá, cognate with Igbo ụgbā.

en-igba-yo-num-6jDOPYFs.etymologyText: From a distinct root unlike most related languages, possibly a late innovation, from i- + gba, but see Nupe gba (“two thousand”)

glosses: A type of rope used for climbing
bitter tomato, Solanum aethiopicum; garden egg, eggplant

en-o_dabọ-yo-intj-UWhMYI5X.etymologyText: From ó (“impersonal third-person subject pronoun”) + di (“to become”) + àbọ̀ (“return”), literally “till I come again”

examples.translation: Did you sleep well?

examples.text: A máa ń jẹ ẹ̀bà dáadáa.
examples.translation: We eat eba gladly.

glosses: thank you (non-honorific, to a singular person)
thank you (honorific, or to multiple people)

en-ẹ_ṣeun-yo-intj-9AugNKOC.etymologyText: From ẹ (“honorific or plural second-person pronoun”) + ṣeun (“to be commendable”).

glosses: thank you (honorific, or to multiple people)

en-o_ṣeun-yo-intj-4MXAHtET.etymologyText: From o (“non-honorific second-person singular pronoun”) + ṣeun (“to be commendable”), an extended meaning derived from ṣe (“to do”) + ohun (“a thing”).

glosses: thank you (non-honorific, to a singular person)

en-kabukabu-yo-noun-wVFqFGQ2.etymologyText: Reduplication of kabú from English cab.

glosses: cab; taxi (in particular) a private car operating as an unlicensed taxi.

en-edekoyede-yo-noun-GGyqCZo8.etymologyText: èdè (“language”) + kò (“negation prefix”) + yé (“to understand”) + èdè (“language”), literally “language doesn't understand language”

en-ẹdun-yo-noun-26kpxT3c.etymologyText: Cognate with Igala ẹ́dọ, proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruba *ɛ-dʊ̃, from Proto-Edekiri *ɛ-dʊ̃, ultimately from Proto-Yoruboid *ɛ́-dʊ̃

glosses: colobus monkey (Colobus vellerosus), known for its deep cultural association with twins

examples.text: ọmọ ẹdun tí ń ṣeré lórí igi
examples.translation: The child of the ursine colobus monkey that is playing on the tree

glosses: thunderbolt; thunderstone, associated with the orisha Ṣàngó

en-ẹdun-yo-noun-AlQS09-A.etymologyText: Cognate with Igala ẹ́dọ̀, proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *ɛ-dʊ̃̀ or Proto-Yoruboid *ɛ́-dʊ̃̀, equivalent to *ɛ́- (“nominalizing prefix”) + *dʊ̃̀ (“to chop”). The verb *dʊ̃̀ likely means to chop or cut down, compare with ké (“to axe”) in àkíké (“axe”)

en-ẹja-yo-noun-tHSpmicF.etymologyText: Proposed to have derived from Proto-Yoruboid *ɛ́-ja, cognates include Olukumi ẹ́zá and Igala ẹ́ja, likely related to Igbo azu

en-ọkin-yo-noun-0UbX-QtR.etymologyText: The ọ̀kín bird originally referred to the white morph of the African Paradise flycatcher, which has extremely long, white wings. It is praised as "king of the birds." Upon the introduction of peacocks to Nigeria sometime in the mid-1900s, ọ̀kín became a neologism referring to the peacock, and now it is widely used.

glosses: African paradise flycatcher, especially the white morph form with white tail feathers; cattle egret

examples.text: Ọ̀kín bàbá ẹiyẹ, ọ̀kín ẹlẹ́wà àlà
examples.translation: Okin the father of the birds, okin, the one with the beautiful white feathers

glosses: peafowl; peacock (peacocks did not live in the range of Yorubaland in the past, and were introduced in recent times)

examples.text: Kọ́ńsónáǹtì méjìdínlógún l'ó wà ní édè Yorùbá: B, D, F, G, GB, H, J, K, L, M, N, P, R, S, Ṣ, T, W, àti Y.
examples.translation: In Yoruba, there are 18 consonants: B, D, F, G, GB, H, J, K, L, M, N, P, R, S, Ṣ, T, W, and Y.

examples.text: Fáwẹ̀lì méjìlá l'ó wà ní èdè Yorùbá. Fáwẹ̀lì àìránmúpè méje: A, E, Ẹ, I, O, Ọ, U, àti fáwẹ̀lì àránmúpè márùn-ún: AN, ẸN, IN, ỌN, UN.
examples.translation: In Yoruba, there are 12 vowels. 7 oral vowels: A, E, Ẹ, I, O, Ọ, U, and 5 nasal vowels: AN, ẸN, IN, ỌN, UN.

en-sababi-yo-noun-P7lx6SUB.etymologyText: From Hausa sabàbī, ultimately from Arabic سَبَب (sabab).

en-tadawa-yo-noun-tyi353X3.etymologyText: Borrowed from Hausa tàdawā̀, from a Berber language, ultimately from Arabic دَوَاة (dawāh, “inkwell”).

examples.translation: It's very tall

en-ọkanlelogun-yo-num-pp7bSJ9O.etymologyText: Contraction of ọ̀kàn lé ní ogún (“one more than twenty”).

en-ejilelogun-yo-num-Ko2qeqx6.etymologyText: Contraction of èjì lé ní ogún (“two more than twenty”).

en-ẹtalelogun-yo-num-Mo5R~K6v.etymologyText: Contraction of ẹ̀tà lé ní ogún (“three more than twenty”).

en-ẹrinlelogun-yo-num-G8vOeA3d.etymologyText: Contraction of ẹ̀rìn lé ní ogún (“four more than twenty”).

en-arundinlọgbọn-yo-num-rDFk1Zxp.etymologyText: Contraction of àrún dín ní ọgbọ̀n (“five reduced from thirty”).

en-Ogboni-yo-name-gdaJoQtv.etymologyText: From ògbóni, from ò- (“nominalizing prefix”) + gbó (“matured, experienced”) + ẹni (“people”), literally “The wise ones”.

glosses: In precolonial Yorubaland, a male secret society of chiefs that performed religious, judicial, and legislative functions, including the advising and checking of a monarch. They were also the main worshippers of the orisha Ẹdan, and in some towns, they were also the cult of the orisha Orò.

examples.text: They consisted of three classes of chiefs, the Ògbóni in charge of administration, Pàràkòyì in charge of trade and commerce, and the Ológun, in charge of security and war, and their leaders were the Ìwàrẹ́fà.

glosses: a dunce, a stupid person, one who receives poor grades
a seller, owner, bearer or maker of mortars

en-ẹrindinlọgbọn-yo-num-YLfR961C.etymologyText: Contraction of ẹ̀rin dín ní ọgbọ̀n (“four reduced from thirty”).

en-ọrọ-yo-noun-dCQfuIN9.etymologyText: Proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *ɔ̀-là, compare with Igala ọ̀là

derivedTerms.english: wise words, words of the elders

glosses: a supernatural fairy or spirit, believed to reside in physical objects and possess people

examples.translation: This child has become a mysterious being.

en-ọrọ-yo-noun-TYqqZPaF.etymologyText: An old Proto-Yoruboid form only maintained in the Ekiti dialect and Igala language, see Igala ọ̀dọ̀, perhaps derived from Proto-Yoruboid *ɔ̀-ɗɔ̀. Some linguists of the Ekiti dialect suggest the r in this word is /ɽ/, differing from the usual /ɾ/

glosses: matters, a concern of great urgency, issue
The plants of the Euphorbia genus, specifically Euphorbia kamerunica, often misidentified as a cactus due to their similar appearances
Any of the various species of cactus, or a variety of other species of the Euphorbia genus and other genera erroneously identified as cactus
The plants Nesogordonia papaverifera and Sterculia rhinopetala of the former Sterculiaceae family

en-Abiọdun-yo-name-izCE-~Vh.etymologyText: Blend of a- (“agent prefix”) + bí (“to be born”) + ní (“on”) + ọdún (“festival, holiday”), literally “One who was born on a festival”.

glosses: a unisex given name meaning “Born a festival”

en-iyalẹta-yo-noun-ZFA-1Foo.etymologyText: From ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + yá (“to borrow”) + ilẹ̀ (“land”) + ta (“to shine”), literally “The act of borrowing sunlight from the ground to shine”.

en-ẹrẹja-yo-noun-rlaVhXyB.etymologyText: According to Débọ̀ Awẹ́, from a folk etymology, ẹrẹ́ jà (“the place where Ẹrẹ́ fought”). Possibly from ẹrẹ́ + ọjà (“market”)

glosses: market square; the central market in a Yorùbá town. It normally opens every five days.

examples.text: ọmọ olúlé ẹrẹ́jà kẹ́ráàbọ̀ ìsinmi ẹyẹ
examples.translation: The child of the house in the central market where you will see many bird nests

en-egure-yo-noun-8i-giIty.etymologyText: Compare with Itsekiri igùrè (“village”), Edo igue, Urhobo ighwre, see Oǹdó Yoruba eguè, probably from Proto-Edekiri *i-gùrè

en-Iṣẹṣe-yo-name-rCALW7L5.etymologyText: From ìṣẹ̀ṣe, ultimately from ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + ṣẹ̀ (“to originate”) + ìṣe (“tradition”), literally “The source of our traditions”.

glosses: The Yoruba religion, the combination of the religious practices and traditions associated with the worship of the orisa and Ifa divination.

examples.translation: Isese is the most senior of the Yoruba institutions

en-Ọsanyin-yo-name-j6PVOpn8.etymologyText:
From ọ̀san + yìn, of unclear origin. A few etymological theories exist:
* An origin myth of Ọ̀sanyìn attributes it from the phrase ẹ̀san ẹyìn (“the reward for palm nuts”). A similar myth is repeated in the Odù Ifá chapter Ọ̀sẹ́ Ọ̀wọ́nrín (#232), where the name is said to come from the phrase ẹ̀sán ẹyìn (“the 9 palm nuts”). Both these myths identify the name as being associated Ọ̀rúnmìlà's role in his birth, with the second myth attributing Ọ̀sanyìn as his younger brother.

glosses: Ọsanyìn (god of plants, herbs, healing, medicine, and magic). He is closely associated with divination and the orisha Ọ̀rúnmìlà.

en-amulu-yo-noun-mnJWbbsT.etymologyText: From à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + mú (“to take”) + lù (“to beat”), literally “That which is used to beat something”.

glosses: The 240 minor signs of the Ifa divination system.
The minor 240 chapters of the Odù Ifá corpus after the 16 oju odu, beginning with Ogbeyẹku.

en-kadara-yo-noun-R1PAjHye.etymologyText: From Hausa ƙàddar̃ā̀, from Arabic قَدَر (qadar).

en-ẹtadinlọgbọn-yo-num-QShm2AA1.etymologyText: Contraction of ẹ̀ta dín ní ọgbọ̀n (“three reduced from thirty”).

en-ejidinlọgbọn-yo-num-lsKoNGGJ.etymologyText: Contraction of èjì dín ní ọgbọ̀n (“two reduced from thirty”).

en-ọkandinlọgbọn-yo-num-oNlnbMWY.etymologyText: Contraction of ọ̀kan dín ní ọgbọ̀n (“one removed from thirty”).

examples.translation: My phone died.

en-atẹjiṣẹ-yo-noun-QMMNm76c.etymologyText: From à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + tẹ̀ (“to type”) + jẹ́ (“to send, deliver”) + iṣẹ́ (“a message”), literally “that which is sent and delivered”.

examples.text: Àtẹ̀jíṣé tí a sẹ̀sẹ̀ gbà láti ọwọ́ ọmọ Nàìjíríà rere kan fi yé wa pé súnkẹrẹrẹ-fàkẹrẹrẹ ọkọ̀ wà láti Ajégúnlẹ̀ sí Mile Two pọ̀ díẹ̀ nítorí òjò tí ó rọ̀.
examples.translation: The text message we have just received from a good citizen of Nigeria informed us that there was a serious traffic jam from Ajégúnlẹ̀ to Mile Two because of the rain.

en-aṣa-yo-noun-VJEre0Jg.etymologyText: From à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + ṣá (“to slash, to strike, to peck”), literally “That which strikes”

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: to slash, to strike, to peck

glosses: A general name for the hawk or kite, but (in particular) the Black-winged kite

en-aṣa-yo-noun-fYwk7yJL.etymologyText: From à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + ṣà (“to select; to be specially chosen”), literally “that which is specially chosen to be practiced”

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: to select; to be specially chosen

glosses: Death (the personified warrior spirit (Ajogun) of death)
Jamaica (an island and country in the Caribbean)

examples.text: Ọ̀rẹ́ mi ń gbé n'ílú Jàméíkà.
examples.translation: My friend lives in Jamaica.

en-ọmọnile-yo-noun-QT3JbZBI.etymologyText: From ọmọ + ní + ilé ("child in the house").

en-ayegbe-yo-noun-8XQQ-Eb~.etymologyText: Compare with Edo ùghègbè, Igbo ùgègbè, Itsekiri ughéngbè

glosses: a mud bed in a home used for sitting and sleeping
inner chamber of a room; bedroom
gate, a short door used to farm animals from entering a house

en-ẹfọnha-yo-noun-WHL2YIJw.etymologyText: From ẹfọ́n (“oil palm midrib's back”) + ìhà (“side”).

en-epo-yo-noun-y5uq7gSm.etymologyText: Compare with Itsekiri ekpo, Olukumi ekpo, Igala ékpo. Proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruba *e-kpo, from Proto-Edekiri *e-kpo, ultimately from Proto-Yoruboid *e-kpo. Also see Ayere ekpú

glosses: Any plant of species Annona senegalensis

en-Abọsẹde-yo-name-pLhOhtoi.etymologyText: From a- (“agent prefix”) + bá (“to join”) + ọ̀sẹ̀ (“week”) + dé (“to arrive”), "One born at the start of a new week", usually given to children born on a Sunday.

en-Ọgbẹni-yo-noun-NLLVGgkK.etymologyText: From ògbó (“old, matured”) + ẹni (“person”), Doublet of Ògbóni

glosses: Mister, Mr. General title or respect of an adult male.

examples.translation: Mr. Akinbiyi
Mr. Adande has arrived.
personal identification number (PIN)
atlas map
Use the chalk to write your name.

glosses: to shock physically, such as with an electric current

en-Kọjọda-yo-name-6rxRIbVn.etymologyText: From kí (“may”) + ọjọ́ (“day”) + da (“to be clear”), literally “May the day be clear”.

glosses: The Yoruba calendar, originally used among the Ìjẹ̀bú people. It originally was a lunar calendar consisting of 4 days, 91 weeks, and 13 months with 7 weeks in each month. The first month is Òkúdù (“June”). It was later modernized to be consistent with the Gregorian calendar
Chicago (a large city in Illinois, United States)

en-jomijoke-yo-noun-MqyjUXIa.etymologyText: From jẹ̀ (“to roam”) + omi (“water”) + jẹ̀ (“to roam”) + òkè (“upper”), literally “To roam the water and above the water”.

en-jomijoke-yo-adj-gzRX6hee.etymologyText: From jẹ̀ (“to roam”) + omi (“water”) + jẹ̀ (“to roam”) + òkè (“upper”), literally “To roam the water and above the water”.

en-oruka-yo-noun-Frl0WDFV.etymologyText: Proposed to have derived from Proto-Yoruboid *ɔ́lṵ̀-ìka, cognate with Igala èlìka, Edo òròká, Izon ụrụká

en-iwu-yo-noun-OLvORTUL.etymologyText: From Proto-Yoruboid *í-ɓṹ, cognate with Igala ímú.

examples.translation: May you use your hand to rub gray hair

en-ile-ikawe-yo-noun-txjxNU9y.etymologyText: From ilé (“house”) + ìkàwé (“act of reading books”), literally “the house of reading books”.

examples.text: Mo ń lọ sí ilé-ìkàwé láti yá ìwé kíláàsì mi.
examples.translation: I'm going to the library to borrow a book for my class.

examples.text: Òkè kelòó ni ilé-ìkàwé ilé wà? — Ó wà l'ókè kẹta.
examples.translation: What floor is this house's reading room on? — It's on the third floor.

en-ile-itawe-yo-noun-ENxAJpoI.etymologyText: From ilé (“house”) + ìtàwé (“act of selling books”), literally “the house of selling books”.

examples.text: Ó lọ sí ilé-ìtàwé láti ra ìwé mẹ́tàlélọ́gbọ̀n (33).
examples.translation: She went to the bookstore to buy 33 books.

examples.text:
DIALOUGE: Délé pàdé ọ̀rẹ́ rẹ̀ Tọ́lá ní ọ̀nà ilé-ìtàwé. […]
Délé: Níbo ni o tí ń bọ?
Tọ́lá: Mó ń bọ láti ilé-ìtàwé. Mo lọ ra ìwé yìí fún kíláàsì Báọ́lójì mi.
examples.translation:
DIALOUGE: Délé runs into their friend Tọ́lá on the route to the bookstore. […]
Délé: Where are you coming from?
Tọ́lá: I'm coming from the bookstore. I went to buy this book for my Biology class.

en-itawe-yo-noun-u1F5hZov.etymologyText: From ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + tàwé (“to sell books”), literally “the act of selling books”.

en-ẹfun-yo-noun-yIb~Efal.etymologyText: ẹ- (“non-gerundive nominalizing prefix”) + fun (“to be white; light”)

en-ọmọba-yo-noun-T3jPeFbG.etymologyText: From ọmọ ọba (“Child of the monarch”).

en-oṣupa-yo-noun-nni0PqAO.etymologyText: From Proto-Yoruba *ɔ̀-cʊ̀kpá, ultimately from Proto-Yoruboid *ó-cù (“moon”) + *kpá, equivalent to o- (“nominalizing prefix”) + ṣù (“to be round”) + pá. pá could perhaps refer to the shining of the moon or the clearness of the moon when it is full. Compare with Yoruba oṣù

glosses: Venus; the second planet in the solar system. Symbol: ♀.

examples.text: Àgùàlà ń bá òṣùpá rìn, wọ́n ní ajá ẹ̀ ló ń ṣe.
examples.translation: Venus and the moon can often be sighted together.

en-onigbameji-yo-noun-noRMTSKa.etymologyText:
From oní- (“owner of”) + igbá (“calabash”) + méjì (“two”), literally “Bearer of two calabashes”
* The picture painted by this term is of someone holding a calabash to contain vomit and another for stool; the two symptoms of cholera.

glosses: sandstone, a generic name for any type of sedimentary rock

en-awọsanma-yo-noun-VmgQELdT.etymologyText: From à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + wọ̀ (“to wear”) + sánmà (“sky”), literally “Covering of the sky”.

en-owusuwusu-yo-noun-ty5cQbRg.etymologyText: From ò- + wúsúwusù, ultimately deriving from an ideophone sense.

examples.text: òwúsúwusù ú gba gbogbo ojú ọ̀run
examples.translation: Fog covered all of the sky

glosses: something that is used to cover one's face or a surface; wool

examples.text: ọkùnrin alárèékérekèé fẹ́ẹ́ fi òwúsúwusù bò wá lójú
examples.translation: The cunning man wanted to use wool to cover our face

en-ikuukuu-yo-noun-zhKCruRA.etymologyText: From ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + kùukùu (“of an entity being opaque or cloudy”), compare with kùrukùru (“fog, mist”).

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: of an entity being opaque or cloudy

en-warakaṣi-yo-noun-w-nNRRVc.etymologyText: *From wàrà (“milk”) + kàṣì (“to become sour, to mold, to become stale”), "Sour milk."

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: to become sour, to mold, to become stale

en-oolu-yo-noun-RYyA1bjO.etymologyText: Contraction of òlìlù, from ò- (“nominalizing prefix”) + lílù (“partial reduplication of lù to beat”)

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: partial reduplication of lù to beat

en-ijapa-yo-noun-Gv9zLg9w.etymologyText: From ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + jàpá (“the motion of one moving awkwardly”, ideophone), literally “That which moves around awkwardly”.

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: the motion of one moving awkwardly

en-takada-yo-noun-OCY1yTJb.etymologyText: From Hausa takàr̃dā, from a Berber language. From Arabic قِرْطَاس (qirṭās), from Aramaic קַרְטֵיסָא / ܩܪܛܝܣܐ (qarṭīsā), from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs). Compare with Nupe tákàda and Zarma takàrda. Doublet of ṣáàtì and káàdì.

en-ajilẹ-yo-noun-dvC9FGnP.etymologyText: From a- (“agent prefix”) + jí (“to wake, to revive”) + ilẹ̀ (“land”), literally “One that revives the land”.

en-Abimbọla-yo-name-NHbuMNUu.etymologyText: From a (“we”) + bí (“to give birth to”) + mi (“me”) + bí (“with”) + ọlá (“wealth”), "I was born with wealth".

en-Ilẹ_kaaarọ-oojiire-yo-name-XS2j4Dg-.etymologyText: From ilẹ̀ (“land”) + káàárọ̀ (“Good morning (Greeting)”) + o (“you”) + ò (“nominalizer, the act of”) + jí (“to wake, to awake”) + ire (“goodness, blessing”). Literally, "Land of the people that greet you good morning, did you wake up well?".

en-Ilara-Mọkin-yo-name-JUaICeVc.etymologyText: From Ìlárá + mọ̀kị́n, ultimately from ìlú (“town”) + Ará (“Ará”) + mọ̀ (“to know”) + ọ̀kị́n (“African paradise flycatcher”), literally “The (people of) the town of Ará know the ọ̀kín bird”.

glosses: Ilara-Mokin (an Ekiti Yoruba town in Ifedore, Ondo, Nigeria)

en-Igbomina-yo-name-1zwiXOFh.etymologyText: From ògbó (“a type of sword”) + mi (“mine, my”) + mọ̀ (“to knows”) + ọ̀nà (“the path, the way”), literally “My sword knows the way”.

glosses: Igbomina people, a subgroup of the Yoruba people
A dialect of the Yoruba language spoken by the Ìgbómìnà

en-Ifadọrọlemi-yo-name-bIDpEYZ9.etymologyText: From Ifá (“Ifá, the deity Ọ̀rúnmìlà”) + dá (“to bestow”) + ọrọ̀ (“wealth, honor”) + lé (“on”) + mi (“me”), literally “Ifá bestowed me with wealth”.

glosses: a male given name meaning “The deity Ifa bestowed me with wealth”

examples.text: mo ń ṣe àtìpó nù ilẹ̀ àjèjì
examples.translation: I am a sojourner in a foreign land

en-ẹmu-yo-noun-CMZfCHuY.etymologyText: From ẹ- (“nominalizing prefix”) + mu (“to drink”). Compare with Olukumi ẹmọ

examples.text: This form of oriki is known as oríkì jáǹtìrẹrẹ, and are normally chanted or sang.
Oríkì ní ó gbajúmọ̀ jù nínú gbogbo ohùn-ẹnu Yorùbá
examples.translation: Oriki is the most popular of the Yoruba oral poetic genres

examples.text: It is often given by one's grandmother or older relative, similar to a cognomen. These often are informal and not part of the official name of a person.
a kì í pe orúkọ ẹni k'á báni wí; a kì í porúkọ odò k'ódò gbéni lọ; bẹ́ẹ̀ náà ni a kì í sọ oríkì ọmọ kínúu rẹ̀ má yọ̀ síni
examples.translation: We do not call someone's name and begin to reprimand him; we do not cite the name of a river and get drowned by it; similarly we do not recite the praise name of a child and he does not rejoice at it

en-Deji-yo-noun-KHMmZga4.etymologyText:
Unclear, several folk etymologies exist. A common folk etymology claims it comes from the phrase "ọwá fadé yìí jì ọ", ultimately from ọwá (“king”) + fi (“to use”) + adé (“crown”) + yìí (“this”) + jì (“to gift, to entrust”), literally “The King gifted you a crown”.
* The title Déjì replaced the original title Àjàpadà. The story attached to this phrase comes from a future Déjì of Àkúrẹ́ being gifted a crown by his grandfather, usually attributed to the Ọwá Òbòkun (king of Ilesha Kingdom), and the title become a nickname that later developed into the title. The story of a grandfather-king giving his future king-grandson is a common story in Yorùbá folklore, see Asunkúngbadé.
Also possibly from Edo Udezi (“leopard hunter”)

examples.translation: Has Toyosi arrived from overseas?

examples.text: Àbúrò mi kan tòkè òkun dé!
examples.translation: One of my younger siblings arrived from abroad!

en-igbalẹ-yo-noun-EAoH0eQ2.etymologyText: From ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + gbá (“to sweep, to broom”) + ilẹ̀ (“floor, ground”), literally “That which sweeps the ground”

glosses: sacred grove where Eégún performers and worshipers meet before a festival or performance

en-ipenija-yo-noun-JHr06vPR.etymologyText: From ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + pè níjà (“to call into question, to challenge”).

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: to call into question, to challenge

en-ọganjọ-yo-noun-l1PLS-Iq.etymologyText: From ọ̀gàn (“dark, severe”) + ọjọ́ (“day”), literally “Dark part of the day”.

en-Agbọnniregun-yo-name-fLRaNwo9.etymologyText:
Several stories from the Odù Ifá attempt to give a folk etymology for this name.
* One states it comes from àgbọn (“coconut”) + ni (“to be”) + ìrègún (“a direct request built on a previous favor one has granted”)
* Another one states it comes from àgbọn (“coconut”) + ni (“to be”) + ire (“blessing, gift, reward”) + Ògún (“the deity Ogun”), literally “The coconut is the blessing of Ogun”

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: a direct request built on a previous favor one has granted

glosses: A praise name (oríkì) or nickname for the orisha Ọ̀rúnmìlà and Ifá

en-Apekẹ-yo-name-lvT6j7c6.etymologyText: From à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + pè (“to call”) + kẹ́ (“to care for, to cherish”), literally “One who is called to be cared for”

glosses: A female oríkì name, meaning "one who is called to be cared for".

en-Awujalẹ-yo-name-3InHMLwC.etymologyText: a- (“agent prefix”) + wù (“to appear”) + jà (“to break”) + ilẹ̀ (“the ground”), literally “The one who appears and collapses the ground”

glosses: Title of the paramount monarch of the Ìjẹ̀bú people and the traditional ruler of the town of Ìjẹ̀bú Òde

en-alakara-yo-noun-D2eI2lhp.etymologyText: *oní- (“one who has”) + àkàrà (“akara”), literally “One who has akara”

en-ẹku-yo-noun-48TktxV8.etymologyText: From ẹ̀- (“nominalizing prefix”) + kú (“to be dead”)

glosses: alternative form of àárọ̀ (“morning, origin, beginning”)

en-ajọ-yo-noun-es42NhN2.etymologyText: From a- (“nominalizing prefix”) + jọ̀ (“to sieve, to sift”)

en-Aderonkẹ-yo-name-r1TesGOi.etymologyText: From Blend of adé (“crown, royalty”) + rí (“to see”) + ohun (“something”) + kẹ́ (“to care for, to cherish”).

en-Ifamugbẹẹ-yo-name-3~P4pPsX.etymologyText: From Blend of Ifá (“Ifá, the deity Ọ̀rúnmìlà”) + mọ̀ (“knows”) + ùgbẹ̀ (“time”) + ẹ (“second person singular pronoun”), literally “Ifá knows your time”.

glosses: a female given name meaning “The deity Ifa knows your time”

en-Ajaja-yo-name-A01g3C8E.etymologyText: From à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + jà (“to fight”) + já (“to snap, to break off”), literally “One who fights and breaks free”.

glosses: A male oríkì name, meaning "One who fights and breaks free".
a praise name or oríkì name for the dove

en-ọkuta-yo-noun-lQ7V6m41.etymologyText: From Proto-Yoruboid *ɔ̀-kʊ́ta, cognate with Igala òkwúta, Edo òkutá, Olukumi òkúta, and Igbo òkutā.

en-uranlọọ-yo-noun-sR-e1Zbp.etymologyText: *ụ̀- (“nominalizing prefix”) + rọ̀nlọ́ọ́ (“to help, to give aid”)

en-iṣẹtọfabo-yo-noun-XiqKVnv4.etymologyText: From ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + ṣe (“to make”) + ẹ̀tọ́ (“rights”) + fún (“for”) + abo (“females”), hence "advocation for women's rights".

balcony

en-iyẹwu-yo-noun-wrTOedPx.etymologyText: From ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + yọ (“to remove”) + ẹ̀wù (“clothes”)

en-adado-yo-noun-UpvBu2ko.etymologyText: à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + dá (“to act alone”) + dó (“to settle”)

en-ayekootọ-yo-noun-oyCCzzpN.etymologyText: From ayé (“world”) + kọ (“to reject”) + òótọ́ (“truth”), literally “The world rejects the truth”.

en-Ọbatala-yo-name-ZkKC-NZM.etymologyText:
It likely originated as a title for the leader of the Mega-House Ìdèta, a polity of the ancient town of Ufẹ̀ during the 9th-11th centuries AD. One of these leaders during the 11th century AD later rose as the head of all the mega-houses in Ufẹ̀ and established the Ufẹ̀ confederacy, a precursor to the Ife kingdom, and served as the chief priest of the deity Ọ̀ràm̀fẹ̀. It was this specific "Ọbàtálá" that became deified as the divinity Òrìṣà (Òrìṣàńlá). The term matches similar structures with titles of chiefs and legendary figures who likely lived as fellow Mega-house leaders and chiefs during that period, such as Ọbalálẹ̀, the head of the Ìlálẹ̀ house, Ọbalésùn, the head of the Ìlésùn house, and Ọbalíá, the head of the Ìlià house. They served as chiefs under the political leadership of the Ọbàtálá, the ruler of the Ìdèta house that encompassed these three minor houses.
* Also see other titles used at the time, Ọbàlùfọ̀n, Ọbalúfẹ̀, Ọbadìo, and Ọbalọọran.
The first part of the term comes from ọba (“king, father”), and the concluding syllable likely coming from lá (“to be big”), thus likely originating from may come from the phrase ọba Ìdèta lá (“The mighty king of Ìdèta”)

glosses: the title of the leader of the ancient Ufẹ̀ mega-house polity, Ìdèta. One of these leaders was later made king of the Ufẹ̀ confederacy of houses and deified as the deity Ọbàtálá

en-aafin-yo-noun-7iqkSAW1.etymologyText: Cognates include Itsekiri àghọ̀fẹn, Ìjẹ̀bú Yoruba àwọ̀fi. Proposed to be derived Proto-Yoruba *à-wɔ̀fɪ̃, from Proto-Edekiri *à-ɣɔ̀fɪ̃. The Proto-Yoruboid term is unclear, see Igala éfọfẹ (“palace”), Igala ọ́fẹ (“chieftaincy title”). Here we see a shifting of /ɣ/ and /w/ to /f/ or vice versa, which, while it is not clear which direction that sound change may have taken, is seen in other Yoruboid or Edekiri cognates, see ehoro vs. afolo and ọ̀fàfà vs. awàwà. See perhaps ultimately from Proto-Yoruboid *á-fɔ̀fɪ̃, *ɛ́-fɔ̀fɪ̃ or Proto-Yoruboid *á-ɣɔ̀fɪ̃, *ɛ́-ɣɔ̀fɪ̃. Also see Proto-Yoruboid *-fɪ̃ (“root relating to royalty or nobility”). Likely a Doublet of Ọlọ́fịn, Doublet of ọfịn, Doublet of Ọ̀dọ̀fin

en-origho-yo-noun-ny5tM6Nx.etymologyText: Cognates include Itsekiri orígho, Igala ójí proposed to be derived from Proto-Edekiri *o-ríɣo, *o-rí, ultimately from Proto-Yoruboid *ó-ɗí, *ó-rí. The compounding of the suffix "ɣo" (later "wo") is possibly an Proto-Edekiri innovation still maintained in a majority of Edekiri languages, and the non-suffixed version likely existed side by side. However, Ayere ago may suggest it is a remnant of an older root. See potential non-Yoruboid cognates, Arigidi igíri, Proto-Bantu *mʊ̀tʊ́è, Proto-Grassfields *tú, Proto-Plateau *-tii, Proto-Benue-Congo *-to, possibly Igbo isi, Akpes ìcùm, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Atlantic-Congo *-li- or Proto-Niger-Congo *-túi, *-tu

en-Ọbalufọn-yo-name-szZEE~YB.etymologyText:
Perhaps from ọba (“father, king”) + ni (“to be”) + ù- (“nominalizing prefix”) + fọ̀n (“to set out for a place”), literally “The King is the one who sets out for new territories” or ọba (“father, king”) + ni (“to be”) + Ẹ̀fọ̀n (“Efon town”), literally “The king at Ẹ̀fọ̀n”. The term fọ̀n relates to setting out and establishing a town, which is commonly attributed to Ọbàlùfọ̀n's reign in Ifẹ̀ and military conquests in Èkìtì and Ìgbómìnà regions. In addition, fọ̀n is a term specific to Central Yoruba dialect. The use of ọba as a prefix in the titles of kings and chiefs is very common in ancient Ifẹ̀, see Ọbàtálá, Ọbalúfẹ̀, Ọbamakin, Ọbadìo, etc. Ọbànìfọ̀n is closely associated with the Yoruba town of Ẹ̀fọ̀n-Alààyè
Often confused with the deity Olúfọ́n, who is associated with Ọbàtálá

A title associated with two legendary figures in Yoruba history, Obalufon Alayemore and Ọbàlùfọ̀n Ògbógbódirin, whom are regarded as being Ọọ̀ni of Ife. They are believed to be descendants of Odùduwà and the founders of the monarchies of many Èkìtì towns. Their reigns are believed to be the beginning of the age of bronze art in Ife.
An orisha and deity associated with Obalufon Alayemore, associated with weaving, art, and bronze, brass casting.
