en-Ogunyọlade-yo-name-3syhjr6M.etymologyText: Blend of Ògún (“Ogun”) + yọ̀ (“to rejoice”) + lé (“onto, upon”) + adé (“crown, royalty”), literally “Ogun rejoices on top royalty”.

glosses: a male given name meaning “Ogun rejoices on top of royalty”
a surname, from the given name Ògúnyọ̀ládé
a male given name from Arabic, equivalent to English Muhammad

en-Ọbasanya-yo-name-YlA2L3n~.etymologyText:
*Clipping of Ọbalúayésànyà, ultimately from Blend of Ọbalúayé (“Ọbaluaye”) + san (“to pay”) + ìyà (“suffering”), literally “Ọbaluaye repaid me for my suffering”
*Blend of Ọba (“King”) + san (“to pay”) + ìyà (“suffering”), literally “The King repaid me for my suffering”

glosses: a male given name meaning “The King repaid me for my suffering or Ọbaluaye repaid me for my suffering”

en-Ọbaluayesanya-yo-name-o4pMdvYl.etymologyText: From Blend of Ọbalúayé (“Ọbaluaye”) + san (“to pay”) + ìyà (“suffering”), literally “Ọbaluaye repaid me for my suffering”.

glosses: a male given name meaning “Ọbaluaye repaid me for my suffering”

en-Olubọde-yo-name-RD2LDN4Y.etymologyText:
*From Blend of olú (“warrior, prominent one”) + bọ̀ (“to come”) + dé (“to arrive”), literally “The warrior has come”
*Clipping of Olúwabọ̀dé (literally “The Lord has come”)

glosses: a unisex given name meaning “The warrior has come or the Lord has come”

en-ọbịtụn-yo-noun-EmH9u7IL.etymologyText: Possibly from ọbị̀nrịn (“woman”) + tịtụn (“new”), literally “New woman”, proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruba *ɔ-bʊtʊ̃ (“maiden”). See Ifè àbitɔ̃

glosses: virgin, a recently married woman who has not had children

examples.translation: The Chief Ajagun met my mother as a virgin

glosses: a male given name meaning “The deity Ifa bestowed me with wealth”
a surname, from the given name Fádọ́rọ̀lémi
to be lukewarm, to be tepid

examples.text: Ṣé ìyá ẹ ti débùúté lálàáfíà?
examples.translation: Did your mum reach her destination safely?

glosses: An important Yoruba religious process and ceremony performed for a newborn child.

examples.text: It consists of three parts, a ceremony to aid a couple who is struggling to have children, then a ceremony performed while a woman is pregnant to determine if a child is a reincarnated ancestor, and to determine if the child may be an abíkú. Finally, the main part of the ceremony is performed for a child within the first week of their birth. It consists of the consulting of Ifá by a babalawo to determine a child's destiny (àyànmọ́), future, and also to determine if the child has certain taboos (èèwọ̀). This is said to be done by measuring a child's ògo and ìràwọ̀, how glorious and bright a child's destiny is.

glosses: Benin Kingdom (a historical kingdom in Nigeria)

en-Ajogun-yo-name-hNHlgwC7.etymologyText: From a- (“agent prefix”) + jẹ (“to eat, consume”) + ogun (“war”), literally “The ones that feed on war”.

glosses: In the Yoruba mythology, the personification of malevolent forces as six hundred and one warriors that wage war against humanity. The eight leaders of these forces include Ikú (“personification of death”), Àrùn (“personification of disease”), Ẹ̀gbà (“personification of paralysis”), Èpè (“personification of curses”), Òfò (“personification of loss”), Ẹ̀wọ̀n (“personification of imprisonment”), Ọ̀ràn (“personification of trouble, problems”), and Èṣe (“personification of affliction”).

en-ọlọbatala-yo-noun-BT4t9H0Y.etymologyText: From oní- (“one who has”) + Ọbàtálá (“Obatala”), literally “One who has Ọbàtálá”.

glosses: priests or initiates of the orisha Ọbàtálá

A type of powder from camwood, the wood of the Baphia nitida tree. It is used in the traditional Yoruba religion during divination, in which the powder is sprinkled on the ọpọ́n Ifá, and an odù signature is traced in the powder.

en-salubata-yo-noun-BBQ-vRfP.etymologyText: From Hausa salubbà (“slipper”), from English slipper.

en-iẹsi-yo-noun-IJ92QY7O.etymologyText: Contraction of ìrẹsì, borrowed from English rice.

glosses: A large metal or tin bucket

examples.translation: I filled six large tin buckets of water

en-gọlọmiṣọ-yo-noun-Omx-GUFt.etymologyText: Noun sense derives from ideophone sense

en-gọlọmiṣọ-yo-noun-1T1HMFdH.etymologyText: Noun sense derives from ideophone sense

en-aba-ipilẹ-yo-noun-e-t~Slcl.etymologyText: From àbá (“theory”) + ìpìlẹ̀ (“foundational, base”), literally “The base of a theory”.

en-ipin-yo-noun-IzJxZc-9.etymologyText: From ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + pín (“to share out; to divide”), literally “one's lot, one's portion”.

glosses: the act of dividing something into parts

derivedTerms.english: one's personal orisha, orisha of destiny and luck

examples.text: Ìpínlẹ̀ mẹ́rìndínlógójì (36) ló wà nínú Nàìjíríà.
examples.translation: There are thirty six states in Nigeria.

en-awọ-yo-noun-h7p3rRA4.etymologyText: From a- (“agent prefix”) + wọ̀ (“to set, to go down”), literally “That which sets”.

examples.text: Ọ̀kánjúwà kì í mu ẹ̀jẹ̀ ẹlòmíì; ẹ̀jẹ̀ ara ẹ̀ náà ní ń mu
examples.translation: The greedy person does not drink other people’s blood; he drinks only his own.

en-akara_oyinbo-yo-noun-Ms22GRli.etymologyText: From àkàrà (“akara”) + òyìnbó (“European”), literally “European version of the bean cake”.

en-amunisin-yo-noun-Au2hbxl8.etymologyText: From a- (“agent prefix”) + mú (“to make”) + ẹni (“person”) + sìn (“to serve”), literally “One who engages in exploiting a person to work for them”.

examples.text: Ibikíbi tí oyin bá wà lèèrà ń wá a rí.
examples.translation: Wherever honey is, ants will search it out.

glosses: alternative form of òjíá (“The plant Daniellia ogea, myrrh”)

en-saa_ijọba-amunisin-yo-noun-bCNiZh6s.etymologyText: From sáà (“era, period”) + ìjọbá (“government”) + amúnisìn (“colonialism”), literally “The era of the colonial government”.

glosses: colonial era, specifically referring to the era of colonialism by the British Empire in Nigeria
colonial administration, specifically referring to the British Empire's administration of Colonial Nigeria

en-ọgẹdẹ-yo-noun-rmhAAkTr.etymologyText: Cognates include Edo ọghẹdẹ and Igbo ògèdè, Igbo ọ̀gèdè. This may be reconstructed to Proto-Yoruboid if such a term existed for an older food crop not bananas. Bananas reached West Africa centuries after the Proto-Yoruboid language had dispersed, but may have come in contact with Proto-Yoruba speakers. Thus, it is unclear if this term was borrowed and then transversed the many people groups as they traded and came into contact with the banana (see the term kòkódìà), or if a semantic shift occurred (see the term ọkà).

examples.text: ọ̀kín níí ṣolóríi gbogbo ẹyẹ; àgbagbà níí ṣolóríi gbogbo ọ̀gẹ̀dẹ̀
examples.translation: It is the peacock that is the head of all birds; it is plantain that is the head of all types of banana

en-ọlọgẹdẹ-yo-noun-mn99CxW4.etymologyText: From oní- (“one who has”) + ọ̀gẹ̀dẹ̀ (“banana”), literally “One who has bananas”.

en-ekolo-yo-noun-Aw8khzM0.etymologyText: From e- (“agent prefix”) + kòló (“an ideophone that represents a twisting motion”), literally “The one that makes twisting motions in the ground”.

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: an ideophone that represents a twisting motion

examples.text: békòló bá júbà ilẹ̀, ilẹ̀ á lanu fún un
examples.translation: If an earthworm pays homage to mother earth, she will open up the burrows for it

en-mooluẹ-yo-noun-jqHnS~qa.etymologyText: From English mould + ẹ̀ (“it (third-person singular object pronoun)”), literally “mould it”, describing the manufacturing process.

glosses: molue (a type of bus in Lagos)

examples.text: Wọ́n wọ móòluẹ̀ lọ sí Ìkòròdú.
examples.translation: They took a molue to Ikorodu.

en-agidi-yo-noun-DizRGY3D.etymologyText: From a- (“agent prefix”) + gídí (“of being forceful and defiant”)

en-gbọkan_le-yo-verb-ejfn-VMX.etymologyText: From gbé (“to carry”) + ọkàn (“heart”) + lé (“upon”), literally “to carry the heart upon”.

glosses: to trust; to count on; to rely on

examples.text: Kò sẹ́ni tá a lè gbọ́kàn lé.
examples.translation: There's no one we can rely on.

en-ọlọpaa-inu-yo-noun-0EwAHcJ5.etymologyText: From ọlọ́pàá (“police”) + inú (“inside”), literally “inside law enforcer”.

en-ọlọpaa-yo-noun-YSzzcAyf.etymologyText: From oní- (“one who has”) + ọ̀pá (“baton”), literally “one who possesses a baton”, probably referring to the batons the colonial police officers carried.

en-gbẹsẹ_le-yo-verb-pdZ4fhnb.etymologyText: From gbé (“to carry”) + ẹsẹ̀ (“leg; foot”) + lé (“upon”), literally “to put the foot on”.

glosses: An orisha worshipped among the Òwu people, deified from three important figures among the Òwu whom all bore the nickname Ańlùgbuà. These are the legendary warrior Akíndélé, a grandson or great-grandson of Odùduwà, who founded the town of Òwu-Kúta, his foster father, who was an ancient hero of the Òwu, and his real father, Ajíbọ́sìn, who served as the first Olówu. All Owu settlements claim that Ańlùgbuà died and descended into the ground in their respective towns, and have yearly festivals honoring him.

en-Akoko-yo-name-w13Gwq1h.etymologyText: A folk etymology states, à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + kókó (“reduplication of kó "to kidnap"”), literally “The ones who were kidnapped”; This is said to come from the fact that many Àkókó settlements were raided and the people kidnapped and sold into slavery during the warring periods of the 1700s and 1800s.

glosses: The Akoko dialects of Yoruba, comprising of the western and eastern Akoko dialects and the Ào dialect.

en-abẹ-yo-noun-E~-7L5u6.etymologyText: Cognate with Igala ábẹ (“pocketknife”), Doublet of ọ̀bẹ, proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *á-bɛ, equivalent to a- (“agent prefix”) + bẹ (“to cut”)

glosses: The similar trees Melia azedarach and Azadirachta indica, of which their leaves are used in herbal drinks known as (àgbo).

en-rọparọsẹ-yo-noun-xAcGPHKK.etymologyText: From rọ (“to paralyse”) + apá (“arm”) + rọ (“to paralyse”) + ẹsẹ̀ (“leg”).

en-Bẹnẹ-yo-name--DwU3-De.etymologyText:
From French Bénin
* The country derives its name from the Benin Empire, in Portuguese Benim, from Yoruba Ìbìní the exonym for the empire which according to folklore was derived from the name Ilẹ̀ Ìbínú (“Land of vexation”).

en-ọti-yo-noun--ixw5org.etymologyText: From Proto-Yoruboid *ɔ́-tɪ̃́. Cognate with Igala ọ́tẹ́

en-ọtin-yo-noun-vwrjfxnx.etymologyText: Proposed to be derive from Proto-Yoruboid *ɔ́-tɪ̃́, see Igala ọ́tẹ́

glosses: An orisha in the Yoruba religion, she is worshipped in the town, Ìníṣà, where she is believed to be their main protector. She is the main spirit of the Ọ̀tìn river

en-Oriṣa-nla-yo-name-Ftjg1quP.etymologyText: From òrìṣà (“orisha”) + ńlá (“big, mighty”), literally “The Great Orisha”.

glosses: A nickname or oríkì name for the divinity Ọbàtálá

en-Oriṣanla-yo-name-aj56TXj9.etymologyText: From òrìṣà (“orisha”) + ńlá (“big, mighty”), literally “The Great Orisha”.

glosses: alternative form of Òrìṣà-ńlá (“A nickname or oríkì name for the orisha Ọbàtálá”)

en-Oriṣaala-yo-name-aj56TXj9.etymologyText: From òrìṣà (“orisha”) + ńlá (“big, mighty”), literally “The Great Orisha”.

glosses: alternative form of Òrìṣà-ńlá (“A nickname or oríkì name for the orisha Ọbàtálá”)

en-Ooṣanla-yo-name-aj56TXj9.etymologyText: From òòṣà (“orisha”) + ńlá (“big, mighty”), literally “The Great Orisha”.

glosses: alternative form of Òrìṣà-ńlá (“A nickname or oríkì name for the orisha Ọbàtálá”)

en-Ooṣaala-yo-name-aj56TXj9.etymologyText: From òòṣà (“orisha”) + ńlá (“big, mighty”), literally “The Great Orisha”.

glosses: alternative form of Òrìṣà-ńlá (“A nickname or oríkì name for the orisha Ọbàtálá”)

en-Ooṣa-nla-yo-name-aj56TXj9.etymologyText: From òòṣà (“orisha”) + ńlá (“big, mighty”), literally “The Great Orisha”.

glosses: alternative form of Òrìṣà-ńlá (“A nickname or oríkì name for the orisha Ọbàtálá”)
alternative form of Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì (“Oshosi, orisha of hunting”)

en-Oriṣaoko-yo-name-SvrVCzo~.etymologyText: From òrìṣà (“orisha”) + oko (“agriculture, farm”), literally “Orisha of agriculture”.

glosses: Oko (orisha), the orisha of farming and agriculture, in his male form, he is regarded as a sorcerer and hunter. The prefix oṣó (“sorcerer”) in many names among the Ẹ̀gbá and Ìjẹ̀bú refers to worshippers of Òrìṣàoko, as well as the prefix ọ̀pá (“staff”)

en-Oriṣa-oko-yo-name-2dp42la1.etymologyText: From òrìṣà (“orisha”) + oko (“agriculture, farm”), literally “Orisha of agriculture”.

glosses: alternative form of Òrìṣàoko (“Oko (orisha), the orisha of farming and agriculture”)
the fruit of the tree Irvingia gabonensis
A mucilaginous soup similar to ewedu, made from ogbono, the seeds of the ààpọ̀n fruit

examples.translation: The tree has developed branches

en-ẹka-yo-noun-q3O0i5U0.etymologyText: From ẹ̀- (“nominalizing prefix”) + kà (“to read, to recite”).

en-igbayẹkẹtẹ-yo-noun-Xcx2VdZz.etymologyText: From ìgbá (“eggplant, garden egg”) + yẹ̀kẹ̀tẹ̀ (“an ideophone describing a physical entity being large, loose, soft, fragile and heavy”), literally “large and heavy garden egg”

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: an ideophone describing a physical entity being large, loose, soft, fragile and heavy

en-iṣu-nikan-kọniyan-yo-noun-dprNEV84.etymologyText: From iṣu (“yam”) + nìkàn (“only”) + kọ́ (“not”) + ni (“to be”) + iyán (“pounded yam”), literally “Yam is not the only thing that can be pounded”.

en-kawọboju-kokoro-yo-noun-x3U5U6Ez.etymologyText: From ká (“fold”) + ọwọ́ (“hands”) + bò (“to cover”) + ojú (“face”) + kòkòrò (“insect”), literally “one that coils the hands to conceal or cover up the face of an insect”.

glosses: woodpecker, specifically the African grey woodpecker

en-akoko-yo-noun-07V~lUYc.etymologyText: From à- + kókó, ultimately Onomatopoeic. See Igala ágbólíkọkọ

glosses: woodpecker, specifically the African grey woodpecker

examples.text: àkókó kì í sọgi tútù, igi gbígbẹ níí sọ
examples.translation: The woodpecker does not peck living wood, dry wood is what it pecks

glosses: A nickname or praise name for a woodcarver

examples.translation: May you bore the wood like a woodpecker!!
The woodpecker shall strike the wood!!

glosses: The plant Newbouldia laevis, its leaves are used to adorn newly crowned chiefs

en-alapaandẹdẹ-pupa-yo-noun-fbukilLK.etymologyText: From alápàáǹdẹ̀dẹ̀ (“swallow bird”) + pupa (“red”), literally “Red swallow”.

glosses: porcupine, specifically African brush-tailed porcupine (Atherurus africanus) or crested porcupine (Hystrix cristata)
porcupine, specifically an African brush-tailed porcupine (Atherurus africanus) or a crested porcupine (Hystrix cristata)
tick, specifically a hard tick of the genus Amblyomma
receipt (written acknowledgement that a sum of money has been received)

en-aṣegbefabo-yo-noun-wcKJtVFm.etymologyText: From a- (“agent prefix”) + ṣe (“do”) + ègbè (“strong support”) + fún (“for”) + abo (“female”), literally “One who shows strong support for the female gender”.

en-Aganjuṣọla-yo-name-R9honePQ.etymologyText: Blend of a- (“agent prefix”) + gan (“to be stiff”) + ojú (“face”) + ṣe (“to make”) + ọlá (“honor”), literally “The one with the stiff face makes honor”.

glosses: a male given name meaning “The one with the stiff face”

en-iyaloriṣa-yo-noun-m50iR~OI.etymologyText: From ìyá (“mother”) + oní (“one who has”) + òrìṣà (“orisha”), literally “A priestess of the orisha”.

en-raisi-yo-noun-IJ92QY7O.etymologyText: From English rice. Doublet of ìrẹsì.

glosses: Contextually, the word may imply ancestors, in relation to the ancestor worship practices of the Yorùbá people.
The orisha of wealth specifically among the Ijebu people, equivalent to Ajé, Yoruba names with the prefix Okú, like Òkúsànyà, refer to this orisha.

en-Korikoto-yo-name-wmBePJ7f.etymologyText: From kórìkóto (“A type of toy or shrine used by children”).

glosses: synonym of Kórì (“A female orisha of fertility and children”)

examples.text: ìbọkúbọ ni ọmọdé ń bọ Kórìkóto; ìgbàkúgbà níí gbà á
examples.translation: If a child offers a sacrifice to orisha Korikoto anyhow, the small divinity accepts it anyhow

glosses: A type of toy, it is regarded as a shrine used by children in the worship of the orisha Kórì, (also known as Kórìkóto).
alternative form of kórìkóto (“A toy or shrine used by children”)

en-Ayelala-yo-name-UM3-CccT.etymologyText:
Said to be from the phrase ayé yìí mà lá ò (“This world is truly a large problem”), ultimately from ayé (“world”) + lá (“to be big, large”)
* This is believed to come from a phrase Ayélála uttered while on Earth before being executed

glosses: A female orisha of justice and prosecution widely feared for her harsh punishments for those who commit criminal offences. She is believed to have originally been a slave from the town of Ìlàjẹ and was executed for a crime she did not commit, and soon was deified as an orisha upon the discovery of her innocence. Her role as a punisher of criminals is comparable to the role of Orò among the Ẹ̀gbá.

en-Bilisi-yo-name-pI2A15O4.etymologyText: Hausa ìblîs, ultimately from Arabic إِبْلِيس (ʔiblīs)

glosses: Ibeji, the orisha of duality and twins; and the protector of twins. The orisha, represented by a pair of twins but sharing one soul, are closely associated with Ṣàngó, who himself was the father of twins in his earthly lifetime.

en-kan-un-yo-noun-jUULwKMC.etymologyText: From Hausa kanwā, cognate with Igbo àkanwụ.

glosses: rocksalt; potash; any series of minerals like natron often used in cooking

en-Aarẹ-ọna-kakanfo-yo-name-pKEuZ241.etymologyText: From Ààrẹ ọ̀nà kakaǹfò, from Nupe kakamfò (“One who has no relatives or interests in a place”)

glosses: The title of the highest ranking chief in Yorubaland. Historically, he was the commander of the Ọ̀yọ́ empire's military.

examples.text: The title is born by people not from the town of Ọ̀yọ́, as a way of preventing the possibility of him overthrowing the Aláàfin.

en-Ọsun-yo-name-Im3kl1n2.etymologyText: From ọ̀- (“nominalizing prefix”) + sun (“to ooze, to flow from”), literally “The one who water flows from”.

en-ọdun_Ọṣun-Oṣogbo-yo-name-w7UJkP-r.etymologyText: From ọdún (“festival”) + Ọ̀ṣun (“Oshun”) + Òṣogbo (“Osogbo”), literally “Festival of Oshun of Osogbo”.

glosses: A yearly festival held in the town of Òṣogbo in honor of the orisha Osun, held in and around the grove and sacred shrine of Ọ̀ṣun, Osun-Osogbo.

en-ọlọṣun-yo-noun-wNVv1s4y.etymologyText: From oní- (“one who has”) + Ọ̀ṣun (“Osun”), literally “One who has Osun”.

glosses: A worshipper or initiate of the orisha Ọ̀ṣun

en-dẹdodẹdo-yo-noun--gcto5S9.etymologyText: From Reduplication of dẹ odò (“to hunt in the rivers”, literally “One who hunts in the river”).

en-ọpalaba-yo-noun-qraOQDDS.etymologyText: From Nupe kpálábá, cognate with Hausa kwalabā.

glosses: alternative form of ọ̀páláńbá (“glass, glass bottle”)

en-ọpalanba-yo-noun-pXbDYrk4.etymologyText: Possibly from Nupe kpálábá or Hausa kwalabā, cognate with either of them.

en-babaganran-yo-noun-~LvNWlm~.etymologyText: From bàbà (“copper”) + ganran (“an ideophone describing something that bursts suddenly”), literally “Copper that is heated and then suddenly bursts”.

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: an ideophone describing something that bursts suddenly

en-ọpalamba-yo-noun-qraOQDDS.etymologyText: Possibly from Nupe kpálábá or Hausa kwalabā, cognate with either of them.

glosses: alternative form of ọ̀páláńbá (“glass, glass bottle”)

en-oiie-yo-noun-RVCDIs0u.etymologyText: Contraction of oríire, from orí (“the orí”) + ire (“rectitude”).

examples.text: Ajá aládùúgbò mi máa ń gbó látàárọ̀ dalẹ́. Ó ti sú mi.
examples.translation: My neighbour's dog barks from morning to night. I'm fed up.

examples.text: Kì í ṣe gbogbo ajá tó bá gbóni lọ́jà, là ń dá lóhùn.
examples.translation: It's not all the dogs that bark at one at the marketplace that one responds to.

en-gbo-yo-verb-xFuq9GTP.etymologyText: Perhaps related to Igbo gboo (“early, ancient”)

examples.text: O ò ní tètè gbó, wàá pẹ́ láyé.
examples.translation: You won't age fast, you'll live long.
The corn is not yet ripe

examples.text: Fi ọwọ́ rẹ gbo ara wọn fún nǹkan bí ààbọ̀ ìṣẹ́jú.
examples.translation: Keep rubbing for at least 20 seconds.

examples.text: Mo gbo igi kí èso ré.
examples.translation: I shook the tree so the fruit would fall.

glosses: to trouble; to take its toll

examples.translation: My absence from home 'affected her.

examples.text: Àìsàn náà ṣì ń gbò wá
examples.translation: That sickness is still troubling us.

examples.text: Ikú rẹ̀ gbò wá jìgìjìgì, níwọ̀n bí ó ti bà wá lọ́kàn jẹ́, tí ó sì sọ wá di aláìní.
examples.translation: His death was a terrible blow, since it left us heartbroken as well as destitute.

en-Eledumare-yo-name-AL1mVaFp.etymologyText: From oní- (“one who has”) + èdùmarè (“universe”), literally “One who has the universe”, see Olódùmarè.

glosses: alternative form of Olódùmarè (“the Supreme being in the Yoruba religion”)

en-Eledua-yo-name-qZjdpr-B.etymologyText: From oní- (“one who has”) + edù (“source”) + ìwà (“existence”), literally “The one who is the source of existence”.

glosses: alternative form of Elédùwà (“the Supreme being in the Yoruba religion”)

en-obinrin-yo-noun-PuuM7Va~.etymologyText: Etymology is uncertain, several linguistic hypotheses exist. It is proposed to derive from Proto-Yoruboid *ɔ́-bɪ̃̀rɪ̃, this form still exists in Central Yoruba dialects. Akinkugbe suggests it may be equivalent to abo (“female”) + ẹni (“person”). The consonant /b/ exists in several basic female words, including òbò (“vagina”), abo (“female”).

examples.text: bí ọkùnrín bá rí ejò, tí obìnrin sì pa á, kò burú; kí ejò ṣáà má ti lọ
examples.translation: If a man sees a snake, and a woman kills it, that is not bad; the important thing is for the snake not to escape

examples.text: èyí t'ó wù ẹ́ kò wù mí ni kò jẹ́ k'á pawó pọ̀ láti fẹ́ obìnrin
examples.translation: What appeals to you may not appeal to me, this is why we cannot pool our financial resources together to marry one wife

en-ọkunrin-yo-noun-6yx-fOCd.etymologyText: It is proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *ɔ́-kʊ̃rɪ̃, this form remains the same in Central Yoruba dialects. Cognate with Arigidi ọkọ́ọrẹ. Akinkugbe suggests it may be equivalent to ọkọ (“man”) + ẹni (“person”), compare with obìnrin. The /k/ consonant exists in the roots of many basic male terms, okó (“penis”), akọ (“male”), ọkọ (“husband”)

examples.text: Iná niyì ọdẹ, ẹ̀jẹ̀ niyì oògùn; ká rógun má mà sa, òun niyì ọkùnrin
examples.translation: Just as fire power is the mark of a hunter, so, blood is the mark of a true medicine; and to see a war, and not run away, is the mark of a man

en-Eleduwa-yo-name-2KN1SB48.etymologyText: From oní- (“one who has”) + edù (“source”) + ìwà (“existence”), literally “The one who is the source of existence”.

en-Koso-yo-name-vyvozy7t.etymologyText:
From the phrase Ọba kò so (“The king did not hang”), ultimately from kò (“negation prefix”) + so (“to hang”), literally “The place where the King did not hang”
* This comes from a Yoruba legend in which the location Kòso is believed to be where Aláàfin of Ọ̀yọ́ Ṣàngó hanged himself. After discovering his body, his followers declared to the people that "Ọba kò so," "the King did not hang," and announced that Ṣàngó had not hanged, and instead ascended to heaven as an òrìṣà.

glosses: A legendary place associated with the orisha Ṣàngó, it is believed to be where Ṣàngó in his human form the King of Oyo hanged himself and became an orisha
An area in the town of Ọ̀yọ́ near the palace of Aláàfin where the annual Shango festival is held, and serves as the center of the worship of Shango.
A food eaten by the Ìjẹ̀bú and Rẹ́mọ Yoruba people, made from grated taro (cocoyam), mixed with water, and then boiled. It is normally eaten with a stew like ẹ̀gúsí.

en-agbẹdọ-yo-intj-B87iMPro.etymologyText: From à- (“negation marker”) + gbẹdọ̀ (“must; that which has to be done”)

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: must; that which has to be done

en-Mọremi-yo-name-HnGhqfJR.etymologyText: From Blend of ọmọ (“child”) + rè (“to give attention to”) + èmi (“me”), literally “The child attracts my attention”.

glosses: Also known as Mọ́remí Àjàṣorò, she was a legendary heroine in Yoruba history from the town of Ọ̀fà. She was a Queen of Ifẹ̀, and wife of Ọ̀ránmìyàn. She is known for serving as a spy and warrior whom aided Ife in defeating their longtime enemies, the Ùgbò (Olúyàrè) people. She is also regarded as the mother of the Yoruba people for her willingness to sacrifice her only son Olúorogbo (whom became an orisha upon his death) to the spirit of the Ẹ̀sìnmìrìn river to save the town and guarantee the everlasting protection of the Yoruba people. She was also deified as an orisha upon her death. The town of Ife celebrates the festival ọdún Edì in honor of her and her son.

en-Ufẹ-yo-name--K2ouw7n.etymologyText:
Etymology is unknown, its existence as the first modern Yoruba civilization and kingdom, as well as its role in the Yoruba religion, thus makes it the center of many folk etymologies.
From u- + fẹ̀.
*The verb fẹ̀ is associated with several of these folk etymologies. One suggests it is related to the dialectal definition fẹ̀ (“to be successful, to be prosperous”), since Ufẹ̀ was regarded as an extremely successful and prosperous kingdom.
* Possibly relating to the meaning, fẹ̀ (“to widen”), explained by one of the many origin stories of the Ifẹ̀ kingdom.

glosses: the historic Ife Kingdom, regarded as the first major civilization of the Yoruba-speaking people, it was dominant from the 11th century to 16th century AD. It was known for its extensive wealth, cultural and religious heritage, and trade.

en-palarun-yo-noun-snFSEtk5.etymologyText:
Its uniqueness to only the Àkúrẹ́ subdialect of Èkìtì and lack of semantic cognates in other Proto-Yoruba branches strongly suggests an inter-dialectal borrowing from SEY forms (likely Oǹdó) meaning "lip." Compare with Ijebu Yoruba ùpọ́nrun, Ìkálẹ̀ Yoruba ùpánrun, Itsekiri ùkpárun, Oǹdó Yoruba ùpánún, The "run" part likely relates to roots for "mouth," see Yoruba ẹrụn, while ùpọ́n means "red." Thus, the word meaning "the red part of the mouth," may have caused the meaning to shift from lip to tongue. Fresco '70 also documents an attested Èkìtì form, ụpọ́nrụn, (which has largely been displaced by ètè (“lip”), which may suggest, along with Olukumi ekpùpẹrún and Ede Nago ɛkpɔ̃, a common inheritance of this root from Proto-Edekiri. Also see Ifè bèbèlè-arũ, which is likely a maintenance of the use of the term "mouth" as the base term compounded to make lip.
Further evidence that this is a borrowing can be seen from the fact that this root does not resemble any other Yoruboid root for tongue, and in fact, a synonym, ụọ́n, a term cognate with other dialectal words for tongue, is still used by not only other Ekiti speakers, but other speakers of the Àkúrẹ́ dialect. In addition, "palarun" does not maintain the /ʊ/ found in the word for mouth, likely suggesting the word was borrowed from a language that did not have /ʊ/ in its sound inventory (which is all the SEY dialects)
Borrowing of body parts between SEY and Àkúrẹ́ with slight semantic shifts is attested, see for example Èkìtì ẹ̀tụ̀pá (“foot”) to Oǹdó ẹ̀tìpá (“thigh”). However this root is also found in Ìjẹ̀bú ọ̀pásẹ̀

en-Ija-yo-name-GTopVyTr.etymologyText:
Possibly from ìjà (“fight, conflict”), but the tone shift from low to mid is unclear, and may suggest origin from a root ja. Also possibly related to ìja (“whirlwind”).
Among the Ekiti people, the deity is known as Ụ̀ja or Ị̀ja, and is largely recognized as a brother and close hunting associated of Ogun, while other traditions regard the deity as a female counterpart and the wife of Ògún, representing the male-female dualities of energies in the form of deities. For other examples, see Ṣàngó, Òrìṣàoko and Ọya; Ọbàtálá with Yemòwó, Ọ̀rúnmìlà and Ọ̀ṣun, ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀/ikin divination with ẹ̀rìndínlógún.
The association of a female deity associated hunting is quite peculiar as hunting and war were primarily seen as strictly male professions, but also the duality of male and feminine aspects of hunting can also been seen in deities like Lógunẹ̀dẹ.

glosses: a primordial divinity (irúnmọlẹ̀) and orisha of war, hunting, and fighting. He is closely associated with Ògún and is regarded as his brother along with Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì.
the wife of Ògún, the feminine aspect of hunting

en-agbẹgilere-yo-noun-oEonCsDW.etymologyText: From a- (“agent prefix”) + gbẹ́ (“to carve”) + igi (“wood”) + ní (“adverbial preposition”) + ère (“sculpture”), literally “one who carves wood into sculpture”.

examples.text: Bísí Fakẹ́yẹ jẹ́ ìlúmọ̀ọ́ká agbẹ́gilére, ó wá láti ìdílé agbẹ́gilére tí ó gbajúmọ̀. Bàbá-bàbá-bàbá rẹ̀ ni agbẹ́gilére Ọláwọyin láti Ìlá Ọ̀ràngún. Ìbátan Lámìdí Fákẹ́yẹ ni ó jẹ́. Àwọn ẹbí Fákẹ́yẹ ti gbé àwọn ìṣe àdáyébá ère gbígbẹ́ ilẹ̀ Yorùbá ga, wọn sì ti sọ ìṣe náà ti gbajúgba dé òkè òkun.
examples.translation: Bisi Fakeye is a carver of renown, from a family of famous carvers. His great grandfather was the carver Olawoyin from Ila Orangun. He is cousin to Lamidi Fakeye. The Fakeye family have maintained and developed the carving traditions of the Yoruba people and given them international fame.

en-iyẹn-yo-pron-aV3C1uOP.etymologyText: An intralingual borrowing from SEY spoken varieties into NWY and CY. In some NWY and CY spoken varieties èyinì and ìyẹn are still used side by side, but with ìyẹn gaining ground over èyinì.

en-Ẹmilalẹ-yo-name-SCU-gdjf.etymologyText: Cognate with Igbo Ọmenala (“Igbo culture”), Igbo òmenàànị̀. en-Ẹsinmirin-yo-noun-kPYMaO~y.etymologyText: From ẹ̀- + sìnmìrìn, which in term may be constructed to Proto-Yoruboid *ò-sĩ̀mĩ̀lì. Likely related to Igbo òsìmìlì (“river”), Igbo Òsìmìlì (“Niger river”), and Igala òhìmìnì (“a major river”). The term exists as the name of a river found in Ile Ife, Osun State, until it gradually came to be used as a term for any large body of water, similar to the Niger river. The term was Proto-Yoruboid, but with later language divergences and human migration and intermingling across the West African forest belt, the term diffused and came to be applied to many different large bodies of waters and in various subsets to water itself. The term is still used in reference to the river Esimirin in Ile Ife, Osun State. It is potentially an older cognate with Igbo mmiri (“water”) and thus potentially a Doublet of omi.

glosses: a river or body of water, found in Ile Ife, Osun State.

en-i_si-yo-pron-PHNbHs0w.etymologyText: From ì + sí, probably from the nominalizing prefix ì-, which represents the human form. The use of "sí" can be seen in many interrogative forms in dialects such as Ekiti, see ọ̀kàn sí (“which”), ubi sí (“where”), òlú sí (“how much”), ụ̀gbẹ̀ sí (“when”). en-eyini-yo-pron-aV3C1uOP.etymologyText: From èyí + nị̀, nị̀/nì is used synonymously with èyinì, (compare with yẹn). Used historically among NWY and CY dialects. The opposition between the demonstrative pronouns 'this' and 'that' is expressed by èyí (or èí) and èyinì, nì respectively. In some SEY spoken varieties, however, it is ìyí and ìyẹn. While most CY dialects have maintained it, NWY experience an intralingual borrowing where èyinì was replaced by ìyẹn in academic settings as well as in Standard Yoruba education. Eyini can be seen in older standard Yoruba literature. In some NWY spoken varieties èyinì and ìyẹn are still used side by side, but with ìyẹn gaining ground over èyinì.

en-karibi-yo-adv-tIERwQxl.etymologyText: From kàrí (“where”) + ibi (“place”), possibly from kí (“let”) + à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + rí (“to see”), literally “let us see; let us know”. Kàrí is an interrogative marker," see kàrìgbì (“when”) (literally from kàrí ìgbì, "what time?."). The specific form differs among the different subdialects of Ekiti, but are mutually intelligble. Those in the current Nigerian state of Ekiti may use kàbí or ubi sí, in addition to kàríbi. In the Akure subdialect of Ekiti, they mainly use kàríbi, in addition to kàíbi or kàbí. All these terms are synonymous and can generally used by any Ekiti speaker regardless of subdialect. The root kàrí and the use of sí likely represent different innovations, where one is likely a newer term that are existing together. Kàrí is also used in other CY dialects, such as Ijesha, with kàbí being used by dialects like Ife.

en-Oriṣa-yo-name-YadiJnQj.etymologyText:
The etymology of the term is unclear (perhaps from Proto-Yoruboid *ò-rìsà, Proto-Yoruboid *ɔ̀-rɪ̀cà, or Proto-Yoruboid *ò-rìcà). May have originally referred to the sky or rainfall, a sense which is still used in some contexts but is rare.
Several folk etymologies exist, the main one suggesting it comes from orí (“head, conscience, destiny”) + ì- (nominalizing prefix) + ṣà (“to be selected, to choose”), literally “The head that is specially selected”. (This is unlikely, however, as this term only fits the Yoruba definition of òrìṣà, but not the cognate versions in other languages or even in other Yoruba dialects.)
Historically among the ancient Yoruba, and likely their Proto-Yoruboid ancestors, Òrìṣà referred to a specific arch-divinity of the sky and creation (now known as Òrìṣàńlá and Ọbàtálá). See cognates Itsekiri Òrìtsẹ̀, Igbo Òlìsà, Urhobo Oyise, Yoruba Ọ̀rìṣà, Edo Osa, Oisa, Ebira Oricha, and Fon Lisà. In these related languages and Eastern Yoruba dialects of the Yoruba language (see Ọ̀rị̀ṣà) as well as old Yoruba songs, Òrìṣà has retained a proper noun definition, referring to a specific high-ranking androgynous divinity associated with the sky, creation, and government.

glosses: the supreme being and deity associated with the sky, rainfall, and weather. Equivalent to what is now regarded as Olódùmarè, this meaning is still used in the Ekiti Yorùbá equivalent Ọ̀rị̀ṣà, Àbarị̀ṣà.

synonym of Ọbàtálá, a primordial sky deity or imọlẹ̀ associated with rain, creation, and purity regarded as the oldest of the deities and the creator of humanity. Probably originally equivalent with Sense 1. The deity traditionally was regarded as being androgynous. Their worship combined with the ancestral deification of a figure known as (Ọbàtálá), forming into the Yoruba deity Ọbàtálá and Òrìṣàńlá.

en-ọyan-yo-noun-OBNtbjQ4.etymologyText:
From ọ- (“nominalizing prefix”) + yàn (“to suckle”). The use of yàn with this noun is restricted to Central Yoruba dialects, while others use mu (“to drink”).
Compare with Igala ẹ́nyà, Olukumi ọnyàn, Itsekiri èyán, proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *ɛ́-ɲã̀. Perhaps distantly related to àyà (“chest”) or *ɔ́-yà (“wife”), which links to other Volta-Niger words for woman. Etymological evidence suggests that ọyàn served as a more euphemistic name compared to ọmú, and while it has largely replaced ọmú in common day speech, its original euphemistic origins may support the idea that it comes from a non-anatomical root, similar to the developement of euphemisms for genitalia.

en-oli--yo-prefix-ula4OjM~.etymologyText: From o- (“nominalizing prefix”) + lí (“to have; to own”). The "o" prefix harmonizes with the initial vowel associated with the noun it precedes. Because /n/ and /l/ are allophonic, both oní- and olí- are essentially the same, and in Standard Yoruba, oní- will often have an /l/ when in compounds. However, in certain dialects, the /n/ and /l/ are not allophonic in this case, /l/ is primarily used like in Egba and Ekiti, while in Ondo or Ijebu, only /n/ is used.

en-ụgbae-yo-noun-BXomfmym.etymologyText: From ụgbá (“side”) + iè (“root relating to the human rib”). The first part of this word can be seen in Ìkálẹ̀ Yoruba ugbáyà, and likely means "side," perhaps related to gbá (“to hem the sides of a mat”). The second form is also a root term referring to the rib, in Northern and central Èkìtì dialects, the term is not compounded with anything (Yoruba uè, uyè, iyè). In many other Yoruboid dialects, it is occasionally compounded with something else, see Ondo Yoruba ìghághè. See Olukumi ighè, proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruba *i-ɣè

etymologyMorphemes.gloss: root relating to the human rib

en-akoo-yo-noun-Nw7IIZY3.etymologyText: Its existence in Itsekiri ẹkòró (“hat”) may suggest a borrowing from Oǹdó or Ìkálẹ̀ to Yorùbá or suggests that the term may be of Proto-Edekiri origin, or Proto-SEY-Itsekiri origin. Also see Itsekiri ikoroghẹ̀ (“crown”), and Yoruba àkòró (“coronet”)

a surname, from the given name Adédìran

en-ẹkịkọnnọ-yo-noun-UcEi0fdG.etymologyText: Compare with Olukumi ẹ̀kíkan, Ifè èkíkã́, Itsekiri akikan, Ede Nago àíkã́nã́, proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruba *ɛ̀-kɪ́kɪ̃ã́nã́, *ɛ̀-kɪ́kɪ̃ã́lã́, ultimately a Proto-Edekiri innovation, Proto-Edekiri *ɛ̀-kɪ́kɪ̃ã́nã́, *ɛ̀-kɪ́kɪ̃ã́lã́

en-ọkịka-yo-noun-e-5aJtNz.etymologyText: From ọ̀- + kị̀ka, the root ka can be found in other terms for finger, see Doublet of ìka, Doublet of ùka, proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruba *ʊ̀-ka. en-ẹrọ_ayelujara-yo-noun-KedzmbYx.etymologyText: From ẹ̀rọ (“machine”) + ayélujára (“internet”), see ayélujára for more.

en-ayelujara-yo-noun-BQVNADN8.etymologyText:
From ayé (“the world”) + lu (“pierce”) + já (“to slit”) + ara (“body; itself”), literally “the world has torn through itself”.
The term was originally an appellation for the colonial era coin referring to its pierced centre that was used to string the coins together. The name also referred to the controversy surrounding the demonetization of precolonial currencies and introduction of silver and alloy fiat.
In modern usage the term refers to the Internet's role in creating a Global village.

glosses: colonial era perforated coin, the British West Africa Penny

en-Ẹlẹsinjẹ-yo-name-WUsg6IYW.etymologyText: His role is occupied by Ọ̀sanyìn in most Yoruba settlements

en-Alafẹrẹ-yo-name-DOt6FL4x.etymologyText: From oní- (“one who has”) + afẹrẹ́ (“wind, breeze, cold weather”), literally “Owner of the wind”. Afẹrẹ́ is a term for wind in the Northeast and Central Yoruba dialects. Alafere's role as a female wind deity and female equivalent to a male fire deity takes the form of the deity Ọya in most other Yorùbá towns. Ọya may have developed from Aláfẹrẹ́ worship. In modern times, she is often celebrated simultaneously with Ọya and Ìjùgbẹ̀

glosses: a female deity associated with wind, rainfall, and thunder, and a daughter of the fire deity Ọ̀ràm̀fẹ̀. She is worshipped in Ifẹ̀. She is also closely associated with Ọbaresé the Ife chief deity of rainfall.

en-ọgụnrụn-yo-noun-iQ23mtf9.etymologyText: A semantic shift likely occurred from the human organ known as the neck to simply only neck-like body parts. While it can only be reliably reconstructed to Proto-Edekiri *ɔ̀-gʊ̃̀ɾʊ̃̀, it is descended from Volta-Congo roots for neck, compare with Proto-Kwa *kɔŋgɔ, Proto-Benue-Congo *ton, Proto-Bantu *kíngó, Proto-Gbe *-kɔ, ultimately from Proto-Volta-Congo *ˈkɔtĩ

en-ọdun_Igogo-yo-name-5zXIkeY4.etymologyText: From ọdún (“festival”) + igogo (“bell”), literally “Festival of bells”, as drumming is banned during the festival, with only bells being played.

examples.text: Ọmọ ọwá ají mụ́jà àgbò wẹ́sẹ̀
examples.translation: The child of the king who wakes up and uses ram fat to moisturize their feet

en-gbuyele-yo-verb-bF~7J3s8.etymologyText: From gbé (“to carry, to place”) + uyè (“thought, memory, intelligence”) + lé (“upon, onto”), literally “to place one's confidence upon something or someone”

glosses: a clean-faced person with no tribal marks

examples.text: ṣọ̀bọ̀rọ́ bọlị́là nụ́nụ́ jẹ́. Kí lo máa fịlàkị́là ṣe lójú rẹ
examples.translation: The plain-faced person has made the person with tribal marks upset. Saying, what are you doing with useless marks on your face

en-ọpapa-yo-noun-zB0sLT~j.etymologyText: Cognate with Itsekiri akpakpa, likely of Southeast Yoruba origin borrowed into Ekiti

glosses: harmattan; the strong winds associated with the harmattan

examples.translation: The strong winds that blow throughout the town

glosses: a name for several species of small wild cat, similar to the civet

examples.translation: Idowu the one like the wild cat, the one that carries a tiny piece on the ears

en-ṣẹṣẹ-ẹfun-yo-noun-47FqMsz8.etymologyText: From ṣẹ́ṣẹ́ + ẹfun (“that which is white”)

glosses: white beads, traditional associated with worshippers of the deity Ọbàtálá

derivedTerms.english: that which is characterized by darkness
a group of plants in the genus Cissus

en-ojurọ-yo-noun-5b0IAdEO.etymologyText: From ojú (“surface, face”) + rọ̀ (“to be softening”), literally “The face of the sky is softening”

en-ọdalẹ-yo-noun-Ws4nyG8h.etymologyText: From ọ̀- (“nominalizing prefix”) + dà (“to betray”) + ilẹ̀ (“land”)

examples.text: ikú t'ó ń pa ojúgbà ẹni, ó ń pòwe mọ́ni
examples.translation: when one's peers are dying, it is a sign that one's fate is not too far away
featherless chicken

en-giriwa-yo-noun-m~o5X4wq.etymologyText: Possibly from Nupe giwa (“a salutation for a high-ranking person among chiefs or warriors”)

glosses: president of a club or age-group association
an ancestral fertility deity worshipped in the town of Ọ̀dá, near Àkúrẹ́

examples.text: ọmọ Aláụjọ lọ́tún-ùn, ọmọ Àpàrìkàn lósì
examples.translation: The child of Aláụjọ on the right side, and the child of Aparikan on the left side

en-onile-yo-noun-xKEbOgKn.etymologyText: From oní- (“the one who has”) + ilé (“house”)

en-ọjọ_iwaju-yo-noun-67Peij2a.etymologyText: From ọjọ́ (“day”) + iwájú (“front”), literally “the day ahead/in front”

examples.text: A máa rí ìtẹ̀síwájú náà lọ́jọ́ iwájú
examples.translation: We'll see the progress in the future

en-ṣọkọ-yo-verb-zWOdmVq-.etymologyText: From ṣe (“to be, to do”) + ọkọ (“husband”)

glosses: to be a husband, to be someone's husband
to rule over or dominate a group of people or territory

examples.translation: He ruled over Ekiti and ruled over the Akoko

examples.text: Ó fi okó ṣọkọ Ẹ̀gbá, à á fi òbò ṣọkọ rẹ
examples.translation: You used your manhood to rule over the Ẹgba people, we will now use our womanhood to dominate you

glosses: mane (of a lion or horse); a horse's tail

examples.text: Àgbàrá ọ̀nà Ùgbèyìn ó dúdìí eṣi méè rúgọ̀gọ̀ èyìn í rẹ̀
examples.translation: The torrent on the way to Ugbeyin, it reaches the butt of the horse but I did not see the horse's tail

glosses: divorcée; (literally) a married woman that returns to her father's house

en-Falọdun-yo-name-Ry1-mSw2.etymologyText: From clipping of Ifálọdún, from Blend of Ifá (“Ifa”) + li (“to be”) + ọdún (“year, celebration, festival”), literally “Ifa is celebration”

glosses: a male given name meaning “Ifa is celebration”
a surname, from the given name Fálọdún

en-araye-yo-noun-B2pn10Xd.etymologyText: Composed of the words ará (“people”) + ayé (“world”), literally “people of the world”. This word has cognates in the Yoruboid language continuum with the meaning mainly being that of a single individual, and not humanity as a collective as in Standard Yoruba. It is cognates with Itsekiri irẹ́yé (“person”), Oǹdó Yoruba iáyé (“person”), Èkìtì Yoruba ịráyé (“person”), Ìlàjẹ Yoruba iráyé (“person”)

glosses: humanity, humankind, the world of people

en-aṣofin-agba-yo-noun-hGh3ve~M.etymologyText: Compound of aṣòfin (“lawmaker, representative”) + àgbà (“senior”), literally “senior person who makes the constitution and laws”.

en-ile_aṣofin-agba-yo-noun-P17Vs4qN.etymologyText: Compound of ilé + aṣòfin-àgbà, literally “house of senators”

glosses: senate, upper chamber of a legislature

en-afọju-yo-noun-AuLTsOsz.etymologyText: From a- (“agent prefix”) + fọ́ (“to break, be broken”) + ojú (“eye”), literally “The one with whose eye is broken”. Cognate with Itsekiri afọ́jú, Ifè afɔ́dzú

en-iborun-yo-noun-LTvJSiAj.etymologyText: ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + borùn (“to cover one's neck”)

glosses: shawl; a shoulder sash worn by women

examples.translation: to put a shawl on one's shoulder

examples.text: Fún òde pàtàkì, obìnrin Yorùbá gbọ́dọ̀ ró ìró, ó gbọ́dọ̀ wọ bùbá, ó gbọ́dọ̀ we gèlè, ó sì gbọ́dọ̀ fi ìboorùn kọ́ èjìká. Bi òde yìí kì í bá ṣe òde pàtàkì, obìnrin lè má lo ìboorùn.
examples.translation: For important occasions, a Yoruba woman must tie a wrapper, wear a blouse, wear a gele, and hang a scarf on her shoulder. If the event is not important, women may not use shawls

glosses: a diminutive of the male given name Adébáyọ̀

en-upọnrun-yo-noun-isHvU4HK.etymologyText:
Likely from ù- (“nominalizing prefix”) + pọ́n (“to be red, ripe”) + ẹrun (“mouth”). Cognates with Ìkálẹ̀ Yoruba ùpánrun, Itsekiri ùkpárun, Oǹdó Yoruba ùpánún, archaic Èkìtì Yoruba ụpọ́nrụn. Compare Ọ̀wọ̀ Yoruba ùpẹ̀nmẹ̀nrun, Ifè bèbèlè-arũ, Olukumi ekpùpẹrún, and Ede Nago ɛkpɔn.
See Standard Yorùbá entry ètè for other terms used in the Yoruboid linguistic continuum.

en-otunwa-yo-noun-KeG-dlSk.etymologyText: Compare Itsekiri ùtọ̀gwá, Ìkálẹ̀ Yoruba òtùgwá, Oǹdó Yoruba ùtọ̀gwájú

glosses: Netherlands (the main constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, located primarily in Western Europe bordering Germany and Belgium)
Netherlands (a country in Western Europe, consisting of four constituent countries: the Netherlands per se, Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten the Kingdom of the Netherlands)

examples.text: A máa ń lọ s'íbi-iṣẹ́ l'áago méje ààbọ̀ l'ọ́jọ́ Ajé.
examples.translation: We (usually) go to work at 7:30 on Mondays.

en-iya_iya-yo-noun-HZ9Wyzdv.etymologyText: Compound of ìyá + ìyá, literally “mother's mother”.

en-mama_mama-yo-noun-LG4ZFySg.etymologyText: Compound of màmá + màmá, literally “mother's mother”.

glosses: a male given name meaning “nobility/wealth has resurrected”
a surname transferred from the given name

en-Iṣe_awọn_Apọsiteli-yo-name-cO5KHOim.etymologyText: Calque of English Acts of the Apostles, a calque of Latin Āctūs Apostolōrum, itself a calque of Ancient Greek Πράξεις Ἀποστόλων (Práxeis Apostólōn).

glosses: clipping of Ìṣe àwọn Àpọ́sítélì (“Acts of the Apostles”): Acts

en-Aala-yo-name--aGw0O0j.etymologyText: Borrowed from English Allah or Hausa Allā̀h, from Arabic اللّٰه (allāh).

glosses: alternative form of kankéré (“to fill something up with concrete; eat a lot”)

en-adaja-yo-noun-UcuWx3-j.etymologyText: From à- (“nominalizing prefix”) + dá (“to be alone”) + jà (“to fight”)

en-ẹrọ_abẹbẹ_ifẹatẹgun-yo-noun-bumY9gj9.etymologyText: From ẹ̀rọ (“machine”) + abẹ̀bẹ̀ (“hand fan”) + ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + fẹ́ (“to blow”) + atẹ́gùn (“air, wind”), literally “the mechanical fan that blows air”.

en-amọkoko-yo-name-uBJ-JUMd.etymologyText: a- (“agent prefix”) + mọ (“to mould”) + ìkòkò (“pot”), literally “ones who moulds pots”

en-babaloriṣa-yo-noun-JK0rCst9.etymologyText: From baba (“father”) + oní (“one who has”) + òrìṣà (“orisha”), literally “A priest of the orisha”.

glosses: Forming affectionate or honorific forms of names.

examples.text:
Bọ́sẹ̀ → Bọ́sẹ̀-ọlá
Ibọ́sẹ̀-ọlá, aio rẹ mọ̀ yá ọ ooo. Ibàbá rẹ rọgba okùn, í kúwọ mú yẹra
Bọ́sẹ̀-ọlá your voices strengthens you. Your father bought 200 royal beads, so you can use it to adorne your body. (song during the Aérégbé festival praising a girl performing the ègè ritual)
'Níkẹ́-ọlá ooo, règé ooo, ọlọ́rùn okùn. Ìn ò bó ṣe yí pọ̀gụ̀nrụ̀n, ó ṣèyí ṣèjí ṣara
examples.translation: Àníkẹ́-ọlá, slender, the one with the neck adorned with royal beads. Look at how they surround her neck, she used this and her gap tooth to create her beauty on her body.

glosses: France (a country located primarily in Western Europe)

examples.translation: French person, the French

en-iṣẹnu-yo-noun-GyU6JSAy.etymologyText: From ì- (“nominalizing prefix”) + ṣẹ́ (“to throw away”) + inú (“inside, womb, stomach”)

en-mọ-ọnkọ-mọ-ọnka-yo-verb-kLatID88.etymologyText: From mọ̀-ọ́nkọ (“to know how to write”) + mọ̀-ọ́nkà (“to know how to read”)

glosses: to be literate; to know how to read and write

en-mọ-ọnkọ-mọ-ọnka-yo-noun-V4dWykqh.etymologyText: From mọ̀-ọ́nkọ (“to know how to write”) + mọ̀-ọ́nkà (“to know how to read”)

examples.text: Kí àṣà mọ̀-ọ́nkọ-mọ̀-ọ́nkà tó dé ni ẹ̀yá Yorùbá ti ń ké ewì, irúfẹ́ ewì yìí ni a mọ̀ sí ewì alohùn.
examples.translation: Before the advent of literacy, Yoruba people were reciting poetry, and this kind of poetry is what we know as oral poetry.

en-akalamagbo-yo-noun-skMrU6Zs.etymologyText: From àkàlà (“vulture”) + mọ̀ (“to know”) + ìgbò (“large head; hornbill”)

glosses: a large beaked, scavenging-bird with a goitre, usually associated with the ground hornbill or marabou stork

examples.translation: The ground hornbill does not miss a festival

en-eegun-yo-noun-yNrPZX~p.etymologyText: From Contraction of egigun or egungun. Compare with Oǹdó Yoruba ogungun, Ifè ekũkũ and Igala áchíkwúù. Proposed to be derived from Proto-Yoruboid *V-k'ĩk'ũ.

glosses: a thing that is incompatible or undesirable

examples.translation: The wife chose an undesirable (person) as a husband

en-ojupo-yo-noun-ofzQDfMc.etymologyText: From ojú (“surface”) + òpò (“royal seat”) or ojú (“surface”) + ipò (“position”), literally “the surface of the royal position”
